Schedule

Morning · The main room

9:50The hosts' frame: a moment of rupture, not transitionSam Underwood · Melanie Ormos3Open →

The hosts open the day, which Forward Global holds in partnership with Pictet. They frame the day around rupture and emergence, and ask members to look beyond traditional philanthropy toward a long-range vision and the resources money alone cannot buy.

The day's frame is a moment of rupture, not a gradual transition.

The hosts take the theme from Canada's Prime Minister, Mark Carney, who said in January that the world is in a moment of rupture, not transition. They apply the idea to geopolitics, the environment, technology and culture at once: the world members took for granted is no longer a guide to what comes next. Their provocation for the day is that the next five years could shape the next five generations.Open in session

Every period of breakdown has produced people who built the alternative.

The hosts point to a pattern in history: in moments of rupture, individuals, collectives and communities take risks and make sacrifices to imagine, build, fund and invest in alternative systems, so that when breakdown comes there is something to turn to. They cite the National Health Service in the UK and the civil rights movements around the world, and ask members to see themselves as part of the next such story.Open in session

Funders can work backwards from the world they want in 15 years instead of trying to engineer outcomes.

The hosts suggest that radical uncertainty calls for more than traditional philanthropy, where funders try to engineer outcomes and control the process toward them. Instead, members can picture the world they want in five, ten or fifteen years and work back to the most viable paths toward it. That also means offering resources that are not money, organising through aligned networks, and letting a new identity as changemakers emerge.Open in session

Open the session →
10:10When rupture becomes personalGemma Mortensen3Open →

Gemma Mortensen describes three moments when climate, AI and the collapse of democracy stopped being ideas and became felt. She explains how a year of questions about what we are living through led to New Constellations, and names the four themes every one of its groups returns to.

Rupture becomes real when it moves from the mind into the body.Gemma Mortensen

Gemma Mortensen describes three moments when a crisis stopped being an idea for her. Climate became real when she saw her neighbours' children go to school in gas masks. AI became real when she read a pile of AI science fiction that her head of engineering gave her. The collapse of democracy became real with the assassination of a close friend by a right-wing white supremacist.Open in session

New Constellations grew out of people who could not go back to business as usual.Gemma Mortensen

After returning to the UK in 2019, Gemma Mortensen spent a year asking people what we are living through, what is breaking apart, what is emerging and how to live in times like these. Those questions became conversations, and the conversations became gatherings of people who also could not slot back into the status quo. New Constellations grew from those gatherings, taking communities and institutions on journeys toward regenerative futures.Open in session

Every New Constellations group returns to beauty, nature, love and the harm done by old systems.Gemma Mortensen

Across her gatherings, Gemma Mortensen hears the same themes: the transcendent beauty of a human life; the devastation that old systems of capital, power and technology have brought to the ability to live a simple human life; a profound wish to reinstate ourselves in the web of life and nature; and love in all its forms, from eros and philia to agape and philautia. One group of 24 young people made a candlelit artwork of the different kinds of love.Open in session

Open the session →
A historian's view of emergenceFernande Raine3Open →

Fernande Raine steps back to a bird's eye view of history and finds that many social innovations grew out of rupture. She gives three examples, from the first Axial Age to the aftermath of the Second World War, and names two hopeful signals visible today: young people and collaborative networks.

A historian's long view shows that many social innovations grow out of rupture.Fernande Raine

Fernande Raine says training as a historian teaches you to see the world from a bird's eye view, which also helps an entrepreneur. From that height she looks for patterns and signals of momentum for change. Over the longer arc of time, she finds, humans are able to do remarkable things, and many social innovations grow from rupture.Open in session

Rupture has produced beauty at least three times in recorded history.Fernande Raine

Fernande Raine gives three examples. In the first Axial Age, between 800 and 200 BC, the weakening of tribal life as people connected more widely led to the first ideas of universal morality. After the Thirty Years' War, which she says cut Europe's population by a third [historians put the loss in the German lands, where most of the fighting took place, at between 15% and a third], she points to Baroque ceilings, Vivaldi, Galileo [who died in 1642, six years before the war ended], new navigation and the opening of new worlds. After the industrialised murder of the Second World War came institutions built to safeguard human dignity.Open in session

Two hopeful signals today are young people and networks that reject zero-sum thinking.Fernande Raine

Fernande Raine sees two emergent principles. The first is young people full of hope, desire, love and creativity, and teaching that lets every child who dreams become who they imagine. The second is the power of networks that build communication and collaboration outside the zero-sum mindset. Her question for funders: what if we collaborated radically, with love, generosity and a sense of abundance?Open in session

10:30Table discussions and the four corners exercise
10:50Place, community wealth and two roles for fundersPriya Gupta4Open →

Priya Gupta, an economist, opens with the textbook definition of economics and calls scarcity an assumption. She describes an economy, places and systems that are all ruptured, with the cost of living as the defining issue. She sees a democratisation of wealth and power emerging, points to place-based work already represented among members, and asks funders to act as disruptors and weavers.

Scarcity is an assumption: the economy is a set of human choices, not a fixed law.Priya Gupta

Priya Gupta, an economist, recalls the first page of her first economics textbook: the study of the allocation of scarce resources. She calls all of it human construction. Scarcity is an assumption. Resources are a human definition that undervalues most people, nonhumans and the planet. Allocation is a set of human choices. Calling it a study, she says, hands collective power to something that seems beyond anyone's control.Open in session

The economy, places and political systems are all ruptured, and the cost of living is the defining issue.Priya Gupta

Priya Gupta names the cost of living as the defining issue of our time. Places are ruptured too: high streets are hollowed out and people's connection to place is broken. And systems are ruptured, with extreme wealth and power swaying whole democracies and fundamental rights and freedoms. She treats these as one rupture across the economy, place and power.Open in session

What is emerging is a democratisation of wealth and power, as communities move from being done to to being done with.Priya Gupta

Priya Gupta sees communities taking ownership of the decisions that shape their lives. She points to work already represented among members: a creative youth hub built as a permanent community asset, stewarded by and for young people; the campaign to bring Brixton Market into community ownership, as a matter of culture, belonging, health and democracy; a UK network of hubs reclaiming land, procurement, jobs and finance; a fund backing historically excluded communities; and wealth holders organising to rewire the tax system.Open in session

Funders can act as disruptors who change how money moves and as weavers who link communities.Priya Gupta

As disruptors, Priya Gupta says, funders challenge how money moves and who decides, and back the organising that changes the rules. As weavers, they pool, connect and link people in places, so that what emerges in one community can strengthen many. What is built in place shows what is possible, and organising changes the rules so that it can spread.Open in session

Working groups · Round one

11:30Community Wealth-Building12Open →

Three practitioners on community ownership in the UK: the traders' campaign to buy Brixton Market, community organising that builds power from one win to the next, and what wealth holders can do before and after a purchase.

Place-based work lets funders share power, cross issue silos and see new models in practice

The facilitator gives three reasons Forward Global backs place-based work. Decisions about land, money, energy, housing and work are often made far from the people they affect, and philanthropy has repeated that pattern. Community leaders do not live single-issue lives, so working with them helps funders break out of climate, democracy and AI silos. And a real place shows new ways of being, with real people. Funders often dismiss such work as small, yet it adds up quickly.Open in session

Brixton Market's value comes from its culture, and private equity owners extract that valueA participant

A participant says modern Brixton took shape after 1948, when people who arrived from the Caribbean on the Windrush settled there and called it home. He says its market, nearly 100 years old, has about 170 small traders and some 200 languages. A private equity firm bought it in 2018. Since then independent shops have given way to chains, and each new private equity owner, he says, raises rents and service charges by about 20%. The building is worth more "because it's Brixton."Open in session

Brixton's traders organised to stop their market going to another private equity firmA participant

A participant says that when the market came up for sale, a trader of 15 years drew a line: it must not go to another private equity firm. With wealth holders and groups including the Good Ancestor Movement behind them, the traders made a competitive offer. Lambeth Council listed the site as an Asset of Community Value in July 2026, which made a quick sale harder. In September 2026 the campaign was named preferred buyer, and it is still raising funds.Open in session

Community ownership changes the question from what rent justifies the valuation to who needs the spaceA participant

A participant says the buyer, the Brixton Traders and Community Association, has recently been incorporated as a charitable community benefit society. Every member has one vote, and its board of 12 will have four or five traders, with the wider community in the majority. He says private owners ask what a space must earn to justify the valuation, while a community owner asks who is missing a space and how to fill it. The association will answer to "the people we see daily."Open in session

In community organising, one local victory inspires the nextA participant

A participant follows a chain of wins. He says young women in Brixton formed the Halo campaign and changed their school's uniform rules on Afro hair; the Halo Code that came out of it is a pledge that schools and workplaces across the UK have signed. Some went on to help start Buy Back Brixton. In Coventry and Warwickshire, he says, the community around Grapevine, a disability group that grew out of family-run discos, turned out the day after Warwickshire's Reform-led county council cut disability spending, and the council backed down within a week. He says that group is now buying a building.Open in session

Community organisers listen first and let the issue come from the people they listen toA participant

A participant says community organising starts by listening, never by choosing the issue. He describes an organiser who ran listening campaigns with South American cleaners in the UK. After COVID, the cleaners' deepest fear was falling sick and losing their income, and that fear became the Safe Sick Pay campaign, which he says has since won two of its four demands and safer sick pay for millions of people in the UK. His rule: "The people you listen to are the people you train to become leaders."Open in session

Funders should treat community projects as system demonstrators for the next economyA participant

A participant says the Good Ancestor Movement asks wealthy individuals, families and institutions to move capital from extraction toward a regenerative economy, because much institutional philanthropy is too slow or unfit for this work. She sees Buy Back Brixton as a test of relocalising production and consumption in a community that is already organised. Such work, she says, should be seen as system demonstrators and not as "cute community projects", alongside CIVIC SQUARE in Birmingham and community energy rooted in place.Open in session

Funders and communities build power together more easily when they acknowledge the power imbalance earlyA participant

When Civic Power Fund began, it surveyed every community organisation it knew about its relationship with funders. A participant quotes one answer: "you think we're friends, but if I upset you, you won't fund me." He says naming the imbalance early makes it easier to build power together. Before him, another participant tells a story from Manchester: she asked two wealth holders in her own network for help, at some risk to herself, so that Rekindle could buy its building before a deadline.Open in session

Community change grows like a bazaar, while governments plan like cathedral builders

One member contrasts two approaches. A cathedral is planned from the top: an architect designs it and everyone is paid to build one part. A bazaar starts from a small seed: someone comes, then someone else, and no one knows in advance who will sell what or which relationships will form. In this member's view, government and much of today's work follow the cathedral model, and community change needs more of the bazaar mindset.Open in session

Brixton's market traders already link London to producers in AfricaA participant

One funder taking part says their foundation backs livelihood programmes in Africa that sell to export markets, yet had never connected that work to London. Another participant says the link was not obvious to him either, until a trader in Brixton Village told him most of his products come from Africa, some of them his own. Every morning, he says, a shipment from Africa supplies Brixton's small traders, and that link should be part of how funders support communities globally.Open in session

The fear of misusing power is now a greater risk than stepping in and acting

One member working with community-led groups across Europe says local victories rarely travel across borders: governments make travel hard for Black and brown communities, and funding stays inside national lines. When partners first met online, the member could see their fear lift as they shared tactics. The member argues that being frozen by fear of a mistake is now more dangerous than stepping in and managing the risk, and asks how one local victory can grow into national and then regional change.Open in session

Wealth holders should back a community owner for years after the purchase, and do it alongside othersA participant

One member asks what Buy Back Brixton will need after the sale, when the hard work of running the market begins. A participant asks wealth holders to support the Brixton Traders and Community Association for a five-year period, to build the community's capacity to run it, and to do so with other funders rather than alone. She also asks for support beyond money: telling the story in rooms the community rarely gets into.Open in session

Open the session →
Catalytic capital: the whole spectrum of capital for systems change10Open →

Four contributors and members discuss how grants, catalytic capital and investment can work together for systems change, and why good returns alone do not change a system. The page covers the last half hour of the working group.

Stating your values first lets you apply them to both giving and investingA participant

A participant says being intentional with capital is hard, because it is hard to know what matters to you. Tribe Impact Capital built its Impact DNA process, which uses the UN Sustainable Development Goals to help clients articulate their values. Once those values are clear, they become a golden thread for applying capital across the whole spectrum, whether that is giving or investing.Open in session

Catalytic capital is the unglamorous work of building systemsA participant

A participant does not love the term catalytic capital, because she thinks all capital should work this way. For her it means "the less sexy stuff": the systems. She asks members to put capital where they might not see immediate outcomes, where it can build consensus and support the systems that let more good work happen, including a stronger impact ecosystem in the UK.Open in session

Impact investing is an approach that applies across every assetA participant

A participant says each kind of capital knocks down a different barrier. Philanthropy can fund policy work, catalytic capital de-risks deals to attract mainstream money, and a family office with an operating business can act directly. His one takeaway: impact investing is an approach "that you can have across all of the assets". He adds that the UK impact investing market is growing.Open in session

UK foundations are slightly ahead of family offices in aligning their grants and investmentsA participant

A participant finds that UK foundations are slightly further ahead than families in trying to make their grant-making and their investment portfolios congruent, though some family offices are far ahead. Foundations are also more public, so their experience is easier to learn from. Family wealth is private and complex, which is why he sees peer communities of funders as valuable.Open in session

A portfolio can perform well for 20 years without changing the system around it

One member describes a long record in impact investing with almost no losses. Those investments did great things, but they did not change the system. Working with hundreds of local stakeholders, the member's team has distilled a long list of interventions into a few packages, yet no one has funded the slow work of originating the investments that could follow.Open in session

Catalytic capital is needed before anyone can say what the deal is

The same member says investors ask what the deal is and what the benefits will be, when at the start nobody knows. Large funders compete to fund the problem on the front page and ignore deeper causes. Catalytic capital has different roles at each stage: bringing disconnected stakeholders together, originating investments, building the mechanisms for investing, and the structures that combine finance, technology, skills and knowledge.Open in session

Systems-change models and generous leadership make catalytic capital go further

Another member urges investors to read the systems-change models behind catalytic capital, such as the Water of Systems Change model and network theory, and to ask what leadership model a venture follows, since an ego-driven business cannot be catalytic. Some of the member's favourite investments are around $50,000: enough to get people together, write a report and put a stake in the ground.Open in session

A funder should step back once others will fund the work without themA member

A member describes an additionality test: if someone else would give the million he is giving, "it's time to get off the bus". That takes discipline and setting ego aside, because the people funded no longer need you. On systems change, he adds that it has to be African money for African businesses.Open in session

An impact investor with a mainstream investor's mindset changes very littleA participant

A participant says anyone who works on entrenched issues and is curious, genuine and low-ego ends up thinking about systems, because their money is a drop in the ocean. Access works to bring money into markets nobody wants to fund, packaged so foundations take an interest. She says "there is no point in being an impact investor with the mindset of a mainstream investor", because unless behaviours and incentives change, impact becomes a product to sell.Open in session

Treating wealth as excess money that does not need to grow makes lower returns acceptable

One member names the mental hurdle of accepting 3% for solar panels on schools when an index fund returns about 7%. Once wealth holders see their money as already excess, with no need to grow, accepting 2 or 3% and doing a lot with it becomes exciting. Another member asks where the midpoint sits between concessionary and market-rate capital, since the concessionary pool is small.Open in session

Open the session →
The Information Environment8Open →

A working group on public information: why trust has broken down, what one philanthropy-backed campaign changed in law, and how local news and small community groups can rebuild a shared reality.

Democracy is under strain because trust has collapsed between the state and citizens, between citizens, and in institutions.

One member describes democracy as a set of relationships: between state and citizen, between citizens and institutions, and between citizens themselves. All three are failing at once. Trust in institutions has collapsed, and so, to a degree, has trust in people who do not come from the same place or look the same. Another member adds that democracy cannot function without healthy relationships in those spaces.Open in session

Information has a supply chain like food or medicine, and it has been neglected while political pressure on it grows.

Societies govern the supply chains for food, pharmaceuticals and weapons, but neglected the one for information for a long time, one member argues, and that supply chain is now under attack. In 2024, a senior US politician tied American support for NATO to how Europe treated a platform owner, and a presidential candidate threatened a tech chief executive with prison over the coming election. The member reads both as signs that the contest over information had raised its stakes.Open in session

Philanthropy-backed work on online safety in the UK fed into the Online Safety Act, and a member says it travelled abroad.

Philanthropic funding backed work setting out how platforms could be regulated to protect children and marginalised groups, and that work fed into the UK's Online Safety Act. By one member's account it also informed the EU's Digital Services Act, Australian regulation, a bill now before Canada's parliament and the US Kids Online Safety Act. The plan was a "bank shot strategy": make the law work in the UK first, then use it as proof elsewhere.Open in session

A policy victory has to be defended for years, because implementation is where companies win back ground.

The online safety campaign won its early battles, but the lesson drawn from it is that a new law is only the start. Companies fight over how the rules are applied, and the ground gained in parliament can be lost in implementation. The advice to funders and organisers: "You have to remember, when you have any victories, you have to win the win."Open in session

AI search and summaries threaten people's ability to check what was actually true.

Members warn that AI search summaries give people what the system thinks they want to know, with no incentive to tell the truth. One says access to frontier AI is subsidised by venture capital, so journalists and the public may lose it when prices rise. Another says AI changes material after the fact, leaving researchers and citizens unable to verify the original record. One response under way is a new top-level domain with access controls, meant as a global reserve of knowledge that AI has not altered.Open in session

Local news is democratic infrastructure, and the aim is one reliable source in each of the UK's 361 local authority districts.

Local media did more civic work than anyone noticed while it was strong. As its business model collapsed over the first quarter of this century, democracy, belonging and shared reality all came under pressure. Local news brings people back into a shared reality and helps them hold power to account. A district typically has about 165,000 people, one member says, the size of a mid-sized town or city borough, and about 4.4 million people in the UK live in districts with no dedicated local news outlet.Open in session

Rebuilding local news needs three stages of funding, and the first and last stages are the hardest to fund.

One member sets out a three-stage model. Incubate new outlets from scratch in news deserts. Accelerate the promising ones until they are investment ready. Then catalyse, bringing in impact capital from institutional investors, social investors and government. Incubation comes first but is the harder work, and catalytic capital is the gap that institutions and government are best placed to fill.Open in session

Funding small local campaign groups helps people rebuild trust and hold those in power to account.

Members point to small community groups that fight back where people sense impunity among tech and political elites: parents urging other parents to wait until children are 16 before giving them smartphones, and mothers challenging their local hospital over maternity deaths. Such groups are multiplying across Britain. Members also call for educating MPs and peers on corporate interests, including private equity in public services, and for political finance reform, after one party received £72 million from two donors.Open in session

Open the session →

Working groups · Round two

1:30AI Safety & Power Concentration12Open →

A participant explains why AI is speeding up and why he sees concentration of power as a likelier and more neglected risk than loss of control, and a member presents a member-backed fund built for short timelines. Readers get the options open to the UK, Europe and individual donors.

AI capability at one leading lab is improving about twice as fast as before, METR findsA participant

A participant cites a recent METR report as finding that AI capability improved twice as fast over the past year as expected, mainly because existing models now write about 80% of the code for new ones. [METR's November 2026 assessment covers one lab, Anthropic. It estimates that the lab's models are improving at about twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025, and guesses that about 80% of that acceleration comes from the lab's use of AI in research and development. It gives no figure for the share of code written by AI.] He says this moves the field toward recursive self-improvement, where AI builds better AI around the clock, and that limits on compute and data centres are now less likely to slow development.Open in session

Concentration of power is a likelier AI risk than loss of control, and philanthropy funds it far lessA participant

Most philanthropic money for AI risk goes to making the AI itself safe. a participant argues that concentration of power is both more neglected and more likely: few people want an AI that disempowers everyone, but many want an AI that helps them consolidate their own power. That problem remains even if alignment is solved, and the field is still working out how to define it.Open in session

AI power could concentrate in a few companies, in governments or in two dominant countriesA participant

A participant sees three routes. AI companies could end up producing most economic output by automating labour, which would change the political settlement as well as the economy. Governments, starting with the US, treat the labs as strategic and use AI to widen surveillance. And the US and China could become so dominant that Europe and other middle powers lose any say over how the world is run.Open in session

The UK and Europe can act on AI power through sovereign compute, observatories and civil-liberties groupsA participant

A participant names three options for middle powers. Sovereign access to compute means no other country can switch off access to AI. Observatories can track where power is concentrating and raise the salience of the problem early. And civil-liberties organisations can take up AI in their own work. He calls the monitoring and awareness work cheap to do and a powerful use of philanthropic money.Open in session

Donors anywhere can help start a tenfold increase in independent audits of frontier AI labsA member

A member argues that where donors live does not limit where they can act, and much of the power over AI sits in the US. He says the labs are not transparent and that their most capable models are deployed internally, out of public view. He calls for at least ten times more third-party auditing inside the labs, which philanthropy can start, so that the public and politicians understand what these models can do.Open in session

Data centres make the harms of AI concrete for people today

One member says data centres turn tech power into something everyone can see: emissions that put carbon targets out of reach, higher costs and pollution for nearby communities, the heaviest burden on marginalised communities, and questions about surveillance. Opposition to the build-out unites many movements at once. The same member points to competition policy and the EU Digital Markets Act as tools against present-day concentration of power.Open in session

Fewer data centres in the US slows dangerous AI, but middle powers still need compute of their ownA member

A member holds both views at once. More data centres in the US means more capacity to train more dangerous models, so he wants fewer there. But he does not want the UK, Canada and other middle powers left without compute in an economy that runs on AI. Since the compute will be built somewhere, he would rather it go to democracies with clean energy than to authoritarian states.Open in session

Verification of what runs on data-centre chips can make AI agreements between rival nations holdA participant

Asked whether competition between nations makes AI regulation impossible, a participant says the race is closer to a stag hunt than a prisoner's dilemma: if each side can verify what the others run on their data-centre chips, every side has a reason to cooperate. The technical barriers to that verification are real but solvable, and solving them makes international or bilateral agreements much easier to reach.Open in session

A member-backed AI fund builds what policymakers would need after a warning shotA member

The fund a member helped set up works backwards from a possible warning shot, a disaster that wakes the world up. It backs auditing, AI expertise in US congressional offices, verification technology and a founder designing the body to run an international AI agreement. A participant says people in the EU AI Office told him the institution was not planned before the EU AI Act, and he passes on the founder's insight: "You don't just have the law, you have to have the institution that enforces it." A second strand covers power shifting from labour to compute.Open in session

Donors in AI safety have to choose trusted partners quickly and give at full size the first timeA member

Philanthropy usually spends time mapping a field and making small learning grants. A member says AI does not allow that time: donors have to decide quickly whom to trust and write the right cheque to the right organisation the first time. Partner organisations report funding gaps of tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, and his fund spends each round of funding within three months instead of holding an endowment.Open in session

A youth organisation in Brixton is setting up a community AI lab for young people excluded from mainstream education

One member supports a south London organisation that works with young people excluded from mainstream education and is setting up what the member describes as the UK's first community-powered youth AI lab. The organisation meets young people where they already are: a place they go after school, one of the few neutral places where rival gangs can meet without risk of knife crime.Open in session

The line between today's AI harms and future AI risks is breaking downA participant

A participant says the split between present harms and future risks no longer holds: surveillance infrastructure is being installed now, and AI may reach superhuman capability by the end of next year. Funders who focus on the highest-impact options, or find a trusted adviser, can make a large difference. "The future is not set in stone. There are many different paths that this could take. Some of them are really, really good paths."Open in session

Open the session →
Climate, Nature & Youth Leadership12Open →

A working group on why so little climate money reaches young leaders, and what funders can do about it. Readers get a youth-led coalition's shared ask, a funder's account of changing its mind, and a case for funding the gaps in biodiversity.

Nearly half of Forward Global's members name climate or nature as an interest, while climate receives about 2% of philanthropy worldwide

The facilitator says about half of Forward Global's roughly 300 members name climate, nature, environment or conservation as an interest, yet climate still receives only about 2% of philanthropy. The initiative aims for a world where human norms, behaviours and systems are aligned with a stable climate and the flourishing of the natural world, and it offers a broad tent so members can step in without a fully formed strategy.Open in session

About five funders give most of the environmental grant money from UK funders, in grants too small for whole-system workA participant

A participant recommends the Environmental Funders Network's Where the Green Grants Went report. In her account of its findings, about five organisations and foundations give most UK climate and nature funding, which builds risk into the field. Funding is fragmented, typical grants of 10,000 to 20,000 pounds make whole-system change hard, and transport, waste, the circular economy and oceans are underfunded.Open in session

Youth-led describes who runs an organisation, not the work the organisation doesA participant

A major UK funder turned Another Way down because the funder already backed a youth organisation. A participant asks whether the same funder would refuse a second grantee because it already funds one run by a 50-year-old white man. Youth-led groups range from climate musicals and festival DJ sets to local projects with young people. What the groups share is lived experience and a new way of seeing the world.Open in session

A coalition of about 30 youth-led organisations plans to raise 10 million pounds together over three to five yearsA participant

Young leaders mapped their shared system as a forest and wrote one theory of change around outcomes rather than single organisations. A participant says the coalition is designed for co-founding from the start, built on trust between leaders, and that several co-founders run their groups in the evening after a day job. The first ask is 10 million pounds, shared among the members. Another participant adds that about 30 organisations already work together for free.Open in session

Funders who look for reasons not to back young leaders find those reasonsA participant

A participant says a family foundation listed every reason not to fund young leaders: too small, too risky, too fragmented, too inexperienced. In early meetings with another participant the foundation found evidence for its fears, "because that's what we chose to see". Watching the work grow changed the foundation's mind. Young people will live with the consequences longest, and they join up climate, nature, jobs and democracy.Open in session

Small grants to small projects do not match a large problem, so funders and practitioners should plan togetherA member

A member points to the 30 young leaders who designed their collective in 24 hours of joint work. She argues that giving small amounts to small projects makes no sense for a big issue. A group of funders and a group of practitioners can write the theory of change and the strategy together, and build a model for the work in a short time.Open in session

Synchronicity Earth funds the gaps other funders avoid, and its founders' philanthropy covers the charity's own core costsA member

A member says Synchronicity Earth began with biodiversity and then turned to the gaps: places and species that miss most funders' tick-box KPIs, from the Congo Basin and freshwater biodiversity to marine and Southeast Asian species. Seventeen years on it supports 160 partners on a baseline of trust. The founders' own philanthropy covers the core costs of Synchronicity Earth itself, which lowers the risk for other funders who come in.Open in session

Pooled funds let funders back partners they would not fund directly, and a youth circle helps decide where biodiversity money goesA member

A member describes one Synchronicity Earth pooled fund with 22 partners and 10 funders giving through it. Those funders would not give to the partners directly, but some do once they understand the work. Through the Chrysalis Youth Fund, a funding circle of young people advises on where biodiversity grants go.Open in session

Nature belongs in every portfolio as a baseline, like an insurance policyA member

A member notes that the Global Risks Report ranks biodiversity loss second over ten years, and argues that philanthropy should be the first mover. In her words, "nature touches everything", so whatever a funder's primary interest, supporting the natural world belongs in every portfolio as at least a baseline.Open in session

Climate delay narratives are built on half-truths, so the answer to them has to be complex tooA participant

One member asks whether members should pool money for a simple five-year advertising campaign. A participant answers that fossil fuel lobbying has moved from denial to sowing doubt, with messages rooted in truth: individuals cannot make a difference, it is someone else's responsibility, it is unfair on working-class people. Another Way finds the same narratives in school textbooks, on TikTok and in classrooms, and helps young people take them apart through dialogue.Open in session

People change because of those closest to them, more than because of a social media postA participant

A participant says hate for climate activists on social media pushes young people out of school climate groups, and Another Way's own posts have been taken down. She cites social movement research showing that people are moved by those closest to them: "my family have gone vegan because of me." Community leaders and peers matter more than campaigns.Open in session

Rivers that rise in upland peat have no value in financial markets, which one member wants to change

One member describes a rural place-based project where partners ask what it would take to classify a river system as natural infrastructure, the way roads or data centres are classed. The member says several rivers start in the area's peatland, yet financial markets do not recognise the river system as valuable and it has no protection. The partners also want a programme that finds young local talent and trains it in systems thinking to lead the new models.Open in session

Open the session →
Network principles and practice7Open →

A working group on the four principles of network leadership and how they work in practice, with stories from drone and data labs in more than 35 countries, river catchments in South Wales and a campaign that shares the credit.

High-impact networks share four principles: mission before organisation, trust not control, humility not brand, and constellations not stars.A member

A member finds the same leadership mindset across the high-impact networks she has studied for more than twenty years. People put the mission ahead of their organisation's self-interest and give up control when needed. They govern through trust, finding partners with shared values and then letting go. They share credit generously, which builds a reserve of goodwill for future collaboration. And they build constellations instead of little empires, because social change is complex, emergent and messy.Open in session

Network leaders nudge direction from behind and judge impact by their contribution instead of claiming credit.

One member compares network leadership to "a cowboy at the back of the herd": the herd knows roughly where it is going, and the leader nudges it back on course now and then. Members say impact in networks should be shown as contribution rather than attribution, since relationships are hard to measure and system change often fails. They advise keeping at least one simple North Star metric, avoiding networks that exist only to convene, and collecting data in ways that strengthen the network.Open in session

Flying Labs puts local experts in charge in more than 35 countries, and the network's interdependence makes it resilient.A participant

A participant describes a network of local experts who own, decide on and lead the use of drones, data and geospatial AI in their own countries, and help to finance it. The central organisation stays small because its job is to bring people together, not to control them. Partners are neither dependent nor independent but interdependent, so when a funding shock hits one country, no single node is critical and other partners step in.Open in session

Clear, transparent boundaries let network partners hold each other to account without control from the top.A participant

Flying Labs keeps strengthening its network boundaries: transparent guidelines on what it means to be part of the network. Partners pay a small annual fee for access to shared resources and commit to the network's two values, sharing and collaboration. Each year partners assess themselves against those expectations. A participant finds that peers then hold each other accountable, which works better than oversight from the centre and lets the centre give up decision-making.Open in session

A campaign that hands the credit to its partners builds a broader coalition.

One member describes an online safety campaign that built a wide coalition by giving smaller campaigns free help, including legal advice, and by sending journalists to speak to its grantees instead of to the funder. The member says the method has since been used by campaigns on social media regulation in other countries.Open in session

In South Wales, North Star Transition reframed river pollution as a question of how local businesses work.

North Star Transition set up a Transition Lab that, by the account given in the room, brought together more than 200 stakeholders from farming, the environment, the NHS, energy and transport to decide what they want to change in their region. The lab's framing: "It's not about the rivers. It's about the business practice of people who live around the rivers." The network brought two development banks together, which set up a broad loan for farm transitions, and North Star has never claimed the credit.Open in session

Backing young people's ideas early can build a network of future leaders that a funder only sees years later.

One member describes a fund where young people can bring an idea. Years later, every group the member's network went on to fund was run by someone who had started in that fund. Funding people and leadership early, as well as projects, builds a network before anyone knows it exists.Open in session

Close · The main room

2:40Closing session: a key insight in pairs, and what comes nextMelanie Ormos · Sam Underwood

Chatham House rule: remarks from the floor are not attributed.

Insights by topic

Rupture and emergence11 insights · 2 sessions
The day's frame is a moment of rupture, not a gradual transition.Framing the day

The hosts take the theme from Canada's Prime Minister, Mark Carney, who said in January that the world is in a moment of rupture, not transition. They apply the idea to geopolitics, the environment, technology and culture at once: the world members took for granted is no longer a guide to what comes next. Their provocation for the day is that the next five years could shape the next five generations.Open in session

Every period of breakdown has produced people who built the alternative.Framing the day

The hosts point to a pattern in history: in moments of rupture, individuals, collectives and communities take risks and make sacrifices to imagine, build, fund and invest in alternative systems, so that when breakdown comes there is something to turn to. They cite the National Health Service in the UK and the civil rights movements around the world, and ask members to see themselves as part of the next such story.Open in session

Funders can work backwards from the world they want in 15 years instead of trying to engineer outcomes.Framing the day

The hosts suggest that radical uncertainty calls for more than traditional philanthropy, where funders try to engineer outcomes and control the process toward them. Instead, members can picture the world they want in five, ten or fifteen years and work back to the most viable paths toward it. That also means offering resources that are not money, organising through aligned networks, and letting a new identity as changemakers emerge.Open in session

Rupture becomes real when it moves from the mind into the body.Gemma Mortensen · Framing the day

Gemma Mortensen describes three moments when a crisis stopped being an idea for her. Climate became real when she saw her neighbours' children go to school in gas masks. AI became real when she read a pile of AI science fiction that her head of engineering gave her. The collapse of democracy became real with the assassination of a close friend by a right-wing white supremacist.Open in session

New Constellations grew out of people who could not go back to business as usual.Gemma Mortensen · Framing the day

After returning to the UK in 2019, Gemma Mortensen spent a year asking people what we are living through, what is breaking apart, what is emerging and how to live in times like these. Those questions became conversations, and the conversations became gatherings of people who also could not slot back into the status quo. New Constellations grew from those gatherings, taking communities and institutions on journeys toward regenerative futures.Open in session

Every New Constellations group returns to beauty, nature, love and the harm done by old systems.Gemma Mortensen · Framing the day

Across her gatherings, Gemma Mortensen hears the same themes: the transcendent beauty of a human life; the devastation that old systems of capital, power and technology have brought to the ability to live a simple human life; a profound wish to reinstate ourselves in the web of life and nature; and love in all its forms, from eros and philia to agape and philautia. One group of 24 young people made a candlelit artwork of the different kinds of love.Open in session

A historian's long view shows that many social innovations grow out of rupture.Fernande Raine · Framing the day

Fernande Raine says training as a historian teaches you to see the world from a bird's eye view, which also helps an entrepreneur. From that height she looks for patterns and signals of momentum for change. Over the longer arc of time, she finds, humans are able to do remarkable things, and many social innovations grow from rupture.Open in session

Rupture has produced beauty at least three times in recorded history.Fernande Raine · Framing the day

Fernande Raine gives three examples. In the first Axial Age, between 800 and 200 BC, the weakening of tribal life as people connected more widely led to the first ideas of universal morality. After the Thirty Years' War, which she says cut Europe's population by a third [historians put the loss in the German lands, where most of the fighting took place, at between 15% and a third], she points to Baroque ceilings, Vivaldi, Galileo [who died in 1642, six years before the war ended], new navigation and the opening of new worlds. After the industrialised murder of the Second World War came institutions built to safeguard human dignity.Open in session

Scarcity is an assumption: the economy is a set of human choices, not a fixed law.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

Priya Gupta, an economist, recalls the first page of her first economics textbook: the study of the allocation of scarce resources. She calls all of it human construction. Scarcity is an assumption. Resources are a human definition that undervalues most people, nonhumans and the planet. Allocation is a set of human choices. Calling it a study, she says, hands collective power to something that seems beyond anyone's control.Open in session

The economy, places and political systems are all ruptured, and the cost of living is the defining issue.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

Priya Gupta names the cost of living as the defining issue of our time. Places are ruptured too: high streets are hollowed out and people's connection to place is broken. And systems are ruptured, with extreme wealth and power swaying whole democracies and fundamental rights and freedoms. She treats these as one rupture across the economy, place and power.Open in session

The line between today's AI harms and future AI risks is breaking downA participant · AI

A participant says the split between present harms and future risks no longer holds: surveillance infrastructure is being installed now, and AI may reach superhuman capability by the end of next year. Funders who focus on the highest-impact options, or find a trusted adviser, can make a large difference. "The future is not set in stone. There are many different paths that this could take. Some of them are really, really good paths."Open in session

Place and ownership14 insights · 4 sessions
The economy, places and political systems are all ruptured, and the cost of living is the defining issue.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

Priya Gupta names the cost of living as the defining issue of our time. Places are ruptured too: high streets are hollowed out and people's connection to place is broken. And systems are ruptured, with extreme wealth and power swaying whole democracies and fundamental rights and freedoms. She treats these as one rupture across the economy, place and power.Open in session

What is emerging is a democratisation of wealth and power, as communities move from being done to to being done with.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

Priya Gupta sees communities taking ownership of the decisions that shape their lives. She points to work already represented among members: a creative youth hub built as a permanent community asset, stewarded by and for young people; the campaign to bring Brixton Market into community ownership, as a matter of culture, belonging, health and democracy; a UK network of hubs reclaiming land, procurement, jobs and finance; a fund backing historically excluded communities; and wealth holders organising to rewire the tax system.Open in session

Place-based work lets funders share power, cross issue silos and see new models in practiceWealth-building

The facilitator gives three reasons Forward Global backs place-based work. Decisions about land, money, energy, housing and work are often made far from the people they affect, and philanthropy has repeated that pattern. Community leaders do not live single-issue lives, so working with them helps funders break out of climate, democracy and AI silos. And a real place shows new ways of being, with real people. Funders often dismiss such work as small, yet it adds up quickly.Open in session

Brixton Market's value comes from its culture, and private equity owners extract that valueA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says modern Brixton took shape after 1948, when people who arrived from the Caribbean on the Windrush settled there and called it home. He says its market, nearly 100 years old, has about 170 small traders and some 200 languages. A private equity firm bought it in 2018. Since then independent shops have given way to chains, and each new private equity owner, he says, raises rents and service charges by about 20%. The building is worth more "because it's Brixton."Open in session

Brixton's traders organised to stop their market going to another private equity firmA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says that when the market came up for sale, a trader of 15 years drew a line: it must not go to another private equity firm. With wealth holders and groups including the Good Ancestor Movement behind them, the traders made a competitive offer. Lambeth Council listed the site as an Asset of Community Value in July 2026, which made a quick sale harder. In September 2026 the campaign was named preferred buyer, and it is still raising funds.Open in session

Community ownership changes the question from what rent justifies the valuation to who needs the spaceA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says the buyer, the Brixton Traders and Community Association, has recently been incorporated as a charitable community benefit society. Every member has one vote, and its board of 12 will have four or five traders, with the wider community in the majority. He says private owners ask what a space must earn to justify the valuation, while a community owner asks who is missing a space and how to fill it. The association will answer to "the people we see daily."Open in session

In community organising, one local victory inspires the nextA participant · Wealth-building

A participant follows a chain of wins. He says young women in Brixton formed the Halo campaign and changed their school's uniform rules on Afro hair; the Halo Code that came out of it is a pledge that schools and workplaces across the UK have signed. Some went on to help start Buy Back Brixton. In Coventry and Warwickshire, he says, the community around Grapevine, a disability group that grew out of family-run discos, turned out the day after Warwickshire's Reform-led county council cut disability spending, and the council backed down within a week. He says that group is now buying a building.Open in session

Community organisers listen first and let the issue come from the people they listen toA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says community organising starts by listening, never by choosing the issue. He describes an organiser who ran listening campaigns with South American cleaners in the UK. After COVID, the cleaners' deepest fear was falling sick and losing their income, and that fear became the Safe Sick Pay campaign, which he says has since won two of its four demands and safer sick pay for millions of people in the UK. His rule: "The people you listen to are the people you train to become leaders."Open in session

Funders should treat community projects as system demonstrators for the next economyA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says the Good Ancestor Movement asks wealthy individuals, families and institutions to move capital from extraction toward a regenerative economy, because much institutional philanthropy is too slow or unfit for this work. She sees Buy Back Brixton as a test of relocalising production and consumption in a community that is already organised. Such work, she says, should be seen as system demonstrators and not as "cute community projects", alongside CIVIC SQUARE in Birmingham and community energy rooted in place.Open in session

Community change grows like a bazaar, while governments plan like cathedral buildersWealth-building

One member contrasts two approaches. A cathedral is planned from the top: an architect designs it and everyone is paid to build one part. A bazaar starts from a small seed: someone comes, then someone else, and no one knows in advance who will sell what or which relationships will form. In this member's view, government and much of today's work follow the cathedral model, and community change needs more of the bazaar mindset.Open in session

Brixton's market traders already link London to producers in AfricaA participant · Wealth-building

One funder taking part says their foundation backs livelihood programmes in Africa that sell to export markets, yet had never connected that work to London. Another participant says the link was not obvious to him either, until a trader in Brixton Village told him most of his products come from Africa, some of them his own. Every morning, he says, a shipment from Africa supplies Brixton's small traders, and that link should be part of how funders support communities globally.Open in session

Wealth holders should back a community owner for years after the purchase, and do it alongside othersA participant · Wealth-building

One member asks what Buy Back Brixton will need after the sale, when the hard work of running the market begins. A participant asks wealth holders to support the Brixton Traders and Community Association for a five-year period, to build the community's capacity to run it, and to do so with other funders rather than alone. She also asks for support beyond money: telling the story in rooms the community rarely gets into.Open in session

Local news is democratic infrastructure, and the aim is one reliable source in each of the UK's 361 local authority districts.Information

Local media did more civic work than anyone noticed while it was strong. As its business model collapsed over the first quarter of this century, democracy, belonging and shared reality all came under pressure. Local news brings people back into a shared reality and helps them hold power to account. A district typically has about 165,000 people, one member says, the size of a mid-sized town or city borough, and about 4.4 million people in the UK live in districts with no dedicated local news outlet.Open in session

Rivers that rise in upland peat have no value in financial markets, which one member wants to changeClimate

One member describes a rural place-based project where partners ask what it would take to classify a river system as natural infrastructure, the way roads or data centres are classed. The member says several rivers start in the area's peatland, yet financial markets do not recognise the river system as valuable and it has no protection. The partners also want a programme that finds young local talent and trains it in systems thinking to lead the new models.Open in session

Capital and investment15 insights · 4 sessions

Calling it a study, she says, hands collective power to something that seems beyond anyone's control.Open in session

The building is worth more "because it's Brixton."Open in session

Funders should treat community projects as system demonstrators for the next economyA participant · Wealth-building

A participant says the Good Ancestor Movement asks wealthy individuals, families and institutions to move capital from extraction toward a regenerative economy, because much institutional philanthropy is too slow or unfit for this work. She sees Buy Back Brixton as a test of relocalising production and consumption in a community that is already organised. Such work, she says, should be seen as system demonstrators and not as "cute community projects", alongside CIVIC SQUARE in Birmingham and community energy rooted in place.Open in session

Stating your values first lets you apply them to both giving and investingA participant · Capital

A participant says being intentional with capital is hard, because it is hard to know what matters to you. Tribe Impact Capital built its Impact DNA process, which uses the UN Sustainable Development Goals to help clients articulate their values. Once those values are clear, they become a golden thread for applying capital across the whole spectrum, whether that is giving or investing.Open in session

Catalytic capital is the unglamorous work of building systemsA participant · Capital

A participant does not love the term catalytic capital, because she thinks all capital should work this way. For her it means "the less sexy stuff": the systems. She asks members to put capital where they might not see immediate outcomes, where it can build consensus and support the systems that let more good work happen, including a stronger impact ecosystem in the UK.Open in session

Impact investing is an approach that applies across every assetA participant · Capital

A participant says each kind of capital knocks down a different barrier. Philanthropy can fund policy work, catalytic capital de-risks deals to attract mainstream money, and a family office with an operating business can act directly. His one takeaway: impact investing is an approach "that you can have across all of the assets". He adds that the UK impact investing market is growing.Open in session

UK foundations are slightly ahead of family offices in aligning their grants and investmentsA participant · Capital

A participant finds that UK foundations are slightly further ahead than families in trying to make their grant-making and their investment portfolios congruent, though some family offices are far ahead. Foundations are also more public, so their experience is easier to learn from. Family wealth is private and complex, which is why he sees peer communities of funders as valuable.Open in session

A portfolio can perform well for 20 years without changing the system around itCapital

One member describes a long record in impact investing with almost no losses. Those investments did great things, but they did not change the system. Working with hundreds of local stakeholders, the member's team has distilled a long list of interventions into a few packages, yet no one has funded the slow work of originating the investments that could follow.Open in session

Catalytic capital is needed before anyone can say what the deal isCapital

The same member says investors ask what the deal is and what the benefits will be, when at the start nobody knows. Large funders compete to fund the problem on the front page and ignore deeper causes. Catalytic capital has different roles at each stage: bringing disconnected stakeholders together, originating investments, building the mechanisms for investing, and the structures that combine finance, technology, skills and knowledge.Open in session

Systems-change models and generous leadership make catalytic capital go furtherCapital

Another member urges investors to read the systems-change models behind catalytic capital, such as the Water of Systems Change model and network theory, and to ask what leadership model a venture follows, since an ego-driven business cannot be catalytic. Some of the member's favourite investments are around $50,000: enough to get people together, write a report and put a stake in the ground.Open in session

A funder should step back once others will fund the work without themA member · Capital

A member describes an additionality test: if someone else would give the million he is giving, "it's time to get off the bus". That takes discipline and setting ego aside, because the people funded no longer need you. On systems change, he adds that it has to be African money for African businesses.Open in session

An impact investor with a mainstream investor's mindset changes very littleA participant · Capital

A participant says anyone who works on entrenched issues and is curious, genuine and low-ego ends up thinking about systems, because their money is a drop in the ocean. Access works to bring money into markets nobody wants to fund, packaged so foundations take an interest. She says "there is no point in being an impact investor with the mindset of a mainstream investor", because unless behaviours and incentives change, impact becomes a product to sell.Open in session

Treating wealth as excess money that does not need to grow makes lower returns acceptableCapital

One member names the mental hurdle of accepting 3% for solar panels on schools when an index fund returns about 7%. Once wealth holders see their money as already excess, with no need to grow, accepting 2 or 3% and doing a lot with it becomes exciting. Another member asks where the midpoint sits between concessionary and market-rate capital, since the concessionary pool is small.Open in session

Rebuilding local news needs three stages of funding, and the first and last stages are the hardest to fund.Information

One member sets out a three-stage model. Incubate new outlets from scratch in news deserts. Accelerate the promising ones until they are investment ready. Then catalyse, bringing in impact capital from institutional investors, social investors and government. Incubation comes first but is the harder work, and catalytic capital is the gap that institutions and government are best placed to fill.Open in session

Data centres make the harms of AI concrete for people todayAI

One member says data centres turn tech power into something everyone can see: emissions that put carbon targets out of reach, higher costs and pollution for nearby communities, the heaviest burden on marginalised communities, and questions about surveillance. Opposition to the build-out unites many movements at once. The same member points to competition policy and the EU Digital Markets Act as tools against present-day concentration of power.Open in session

Nearly half of Forward Global's members name climate or nature as an interest, while climate receives about 2% of philanthropy worldwideClimate

The facilitator says about half of Forward Global's roughly 300 members name climate, nature, environment or conservation as an interest, yet climate still receives only about 2% of philanthropy. The initiative aims for a world where human norms, behaviours and systems are aligned with a stable climate and the flourishing of the natural world, and it offers a broad tent so members can step in without a fully formed strategy.Open in session

About five funders give most of the environmental grant money from UK funders, in grants too small for whole-system workA participant · Climate

A participant recommends the Environmental Funders Network's Where the Green Grants Went report. In her account of its findings, about five organisations and foundations give most UK climate and nature funding, which builds risk into the field. Funding is fragmented, typical grants of 10,000 to 20,000 pounds make whole-system change hard, and transport, waste, the circular economy and oceans are underfunded.Open in session
