Young leaders8 insights · 4 sessions
Two hopeful signals today are young people and networks that reject zero-sum thinking.Fernande Raine · Framing the day

Fernande Raine sees two emergent principles. The first is young people full of hope, desire, love and creativity, and teaching that lets every child who dreams become who they imagine. The second is the power of networks that build communication and collaboration outside the zero-sum mindset. Her question for funders: what if we collaborated radically, with love, generosity and a sense of abundance?Open in session

A youth organisation in Brixton is setting up a community AI lab for young people excluded from mainstream educationAI

One member supports a south London organisation that works with young people excluded from mainstream education and is setting up what the member describes as the UK's first community-powered youth AI lab. The organisation meets young people where they already are: a place they go after school, one of the few neutral places where rival gangs can meet without risk of knife crime.Open in session

Youth-led describes who runs an organisation, not the work the organisation doesA participant · Climate

A major UK funder turned Another Way down because the funder already backed a youth organisation. A participant asks whether the same funder would refuse a second grantee because it already funds one run by a 50-year-old white man. Youth-led groups range from climate musicals and festival DJ sets to local projects with young people. What the groups share is lived experience and a new way of seeing the world.Open in session

A coalition of about 30 youth-led organisations plans to raise 10 million pounds together over three to five yearsA participant · Climate

Young leaders mapped their shared system as a forest and wrote one theory of change around outcomes rather than single organisations. A participant says the coalition is designed for co-founding from the start, built on trust between leaders, and that several co-founders run their groups in the evening after a day job. The first ask is 10 million pounds, shared among the members. Another participant adds that about 30 organisations already work together for free.Open in session

Funders who look for reasons not to back young leaders find those reasonsA participant · Climate

A participant says a family foundation listed every reason not to fund young leaders: too small, too risky, too fragmented, too inexperienced. In early meetings with another participant the foundation found evidence for its fears, "because that's what we chose to see". Watching the work grow changed the foundation's mind. Young people will live with the consequences longest, and they join up climate, nature, jobs and democracy.Open in session

Pooled funds let funders back partners they would not fund directly, and a youth circle helps decide where biodiversity money goesA member · Climate

A member describes one Synchronicity Earth pooled fund with 22 partners and 10 funders giving through it. Those funders would not give to the partners directly, but some do once they understand the work. Through the Chrysalis Youth Fund, a funding circle of young people advises on where biodiversity grants go.Open in session

People change because of those closest to them, more than because of a social media postA participant · Climate

A participant says hate for climate activists on social media pushes young people out of school climate groups, and Another Way's own posts have been taken down. She cites social movement research showing that people are moved by those closest to them: "my family have gone vegan because of me." Community leaders and peers matter more than campaigns.Open in session

Backing young people's ideas early can build a network of future leaders that a funder only sees years later.Networks

One member describes a fund where young people can bring an idea. Years later, every group the member's network went on to fund was run by someone who had started in that fund. Funding people and leadership early, as well as projects, builds a network before anyone knows it exists.Open in session

Democracy and information16 insights · 4 sessions
Democracy is under strain because trust has collapsed between the state and citizens, between citizens, and in institutions.Information

One member describes democracy as a set of relationships: between state and citizen, between citizens and institutions, and between citizens themselves. All three are failing at once. Trust in institutions has collapsed, and so, to a degree, has trust in people who do not come from the same place or look the same. Another member adds that democracy cannot function without healthy relationships in those spaces.Open in session

Information has a supply chain like food or medicine, and it has been neglected while political pressure on it grows.Information

Societies govern the supply chains for food, pharmaceuticals and weapons, but neglected the one for information for a long time, one member argues, and that supply chain is now under attack. In 2024, a senior US politician tied American support for NATO to how Europe treated a platform owner, and a presidential candidate threatened a tech chief executive with prison over the coming election. The member reads both as signs that the contest over information had raised its stakes.Open in session

Philanthropy-backed work on online safety in the UK fed into the Online Safety Act, and a member says it travelled abroad.Information

Philanthropic funding backed work setting out how platforms could be regulated to protect children and marginalised groups, and that work fed into the UK's Online Safety Act. By one member's account it also informed the EU's Digital Services Act, Australian regulation, a bill now before Canada's parliament and the US Kids Online Safety Act. The plan was a "bank shot strategy": make the law work in the UK first, then use it as proof elsewhere.Open in session

A policy victory has to be defended for years, because implementation is where companies win back ground.Information

The online safety campaign won its early battles, but the lesson drawn from it is that a new law is only the start. Companies fight over how the rules are applied, and the ground gained in parliament can be lost in implementation. The advice to funders and organisers: "You have to remember, when you have any victories, you have to win the win."Open in session

AI search and summaries threaten people's ability to check what was actually true.Information

Members warn that AI search summaries give people what the system thinks they want to know, with no incentive to tell the truth. One says access to frontier AI is subsidised by venture capital, so journalists and the public may lose it when prices rise. Another says AI changes material after the fact, leaving researchers and citizens unable to verify the original record. One response under way is a new top-level domain with access controls, meant as a global reserve of knowledge that AI has not altered.Open in session

Local news is democratic infrastructure, and the aim is one reliable source in each of the UK's 361 local authority districts.Information

Local media did more civic work than anyone noticed while it was strong. As its business model collapsed over the first quarter of this century, democracy, belonging and shared reality all came under pressure. Local news brings people back into a shared reality and helps them hold power to account. A district typically has about 165,000 people, one member says, the size of a mid-sized town or city borough, and about 4.4 million people in the UK live in districts with no dedicated local news outlet.Open in session

Rebuilding local news needs three stages of funding, and the first and last stages are the hardest to fund.Information

One member sets out a three-stage model. Incubate new outlets from scratch in news deserts. Accelerate the promising ones until they are investment ready. Then catalyse, bringing in impact capital from institutional investors, social investors and government. Incubation comes first but is the harder work, and catalytic capital is the gap that institutions and government are best placed to fill.Open in session

Funding small local campaign groups helps people rebuild trust and hold those in power to account.Information

Members point to small community groups that fight back where people sense impunity among tech and political elites: parents urging other parents to wait until children are 16 before giving them smartphones, and mothers challenging their local hospital over maternity deaths. Such groups are multiplying across Britain. Members also call for educating MPs and peers on corporate interests, including private equity in public services, and for political finance reform, after one party received £72 million from two donors.Open in session

Concentration of power is a likelier AI risk than loss of control, and philanthropy funds it far lessA participant · AI

Most philanthropic money for AI risk goes to making the AI itself safe. a participant argues that concentration of power is both more neglected and more likely: few people want an AI that disempowers everyone, but many want an AI that helps them consolidate their own power. That problem remains even if alignment is solved, and the field is still working out how to define it.Open in session

AI power could concentrate in a few companies, in governments or in two dominant countriesA participant · AI

A participant sees three routes. AI companies could end up producing most economic output by automating labour, which would change the political settlement as well as the economy. Governments, starting with the US, treat the labs as strategic and use AI to widen surveillance. And the US and China could become so dominant that Europe and other middle powers lose any say over how the world is run.Open in session

The UK and Europe can act on AI power through sovereign compute, observatories and civil-liberties groupsA participant · AI

A participant names three options for middle powers. Sovereign access to compute means no other country can switch off access to AI. Observatories can track where power is concentrating and raise the salience of the problem early. And civil-liberties organisations can take up AI in their own work. He calls the monitoring and awareness work cheap to do and a powerful use of philanthropic money.Open in session

Verification of what runs on data-centre chips can make AI agreements between rival nations holdA participant · AI

Asked whether competition between nations makes AI regulation impossible, a participant says the race is closer to a stag hunt than a prisoner's dilemma: if each side can verify what the others run on their data-centre chips, every side has a reason to cooperate. The technical barriers to that verification are real but solvable, and solving them makes international or bilateral agreements much easier to reach.Open in session

A member-backed AI fund builds what policymakers would need after a warning shotA member · AI

The fund a member helped set up works backwards from a possible warning shot, a disaster that wakes the world up. It backs auditing, AI expertise in US congressional offices, verification technology and a founder designing the body to run an international AI agreement. A participant says people in the EU AI Office told him the institution was not planned before the EU AI Act, and he passes on the founder's insight: "You don't just have the law, you have to have the institution that enforces it." A second strand covers power shifting from labour to compute.Open in session

Climate delay narratives are built on half-truths, so the answer to them has to be complex tooA participant · Climate

One member asks whether members should pool money for a simple five-year advertising campaign. A participant answers that fossil fuel lobbying has moved from denial to sowing doubt, with messages rooted in truth: individuals cannot make a difference, it is someone else's responsibility, it is unfair on working-class people. Another Way finds the same narratives in school textbooks, on TikTok and in classrooms, and helps young people take them apart through dialogue.Open in session

People change because of those closest to them, more than because of a social media postA participant · Climate

A participant says hate for climate activists on social media pushes young people out of school climate groups, and Another Way's own posts have been taken down. She cites social movement research showing that people are moved by those closest to them: "my family have gone vegan because of me." Community leaders and peers matter more than campaigns.Open in session

A campaign that hands the credit to its partners builds a broader coalition.Networks

One member describes an online safety campaign that built a wide coalition by giving smaller campaigns free help, including legal advice, and by sending journalists to speak to its grantees instead of to the funder. The member says the method has since been used by campaigns on social media regulation in other countries.Open in session

Networks and collaboration15 insights · 5 sessions
New Constellations grew out of people who could not go back to business as usual.Gemma Mortensen · Framing the day

After returning to the UK in 2019, Gemma Mortensen spent a year asking people what we are living through, what is breaking apart, what is emerging and how to live in times like these. Those questions became conversations, and the conversations became gatherings of people who also could not slot back into the status quo. New Constellations grew from those gatherings, taking communities and institutions on journeys toward regenerative futures.Open in session

Two hopeful signals today are young people and networks that reject zero-sum thinking.Fernande Raine · Framing the day

Fernande Raine sees two emergent principles. The first is young people full of hope, desire, love and creativity, and teaching that lets every child who dreams become who they imagine. The second is the power of networks that build communication and collaboration outside the zero-sum mindset. Her question for funders: what if we collaborated radically, with love, generosity and a sense of abundance?Open in session

Funders can act as disruptors who change how money moves and as weavers who link communities.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

As disruptors, Priya Gupta says, funders challenge how money moves and who decides, and back the organising that changes the rules. As weavers, they pool, connect and link people in places, so that what emerges in one community can strengthen many. What is built in place shows what is possible, and organising changes the rules so that it can spread.Open in session

Community change grows like a bazaar, while governments plan like cathedral buildersWealth-building

One member contrasts two approaches. A cathedral is planned from the top: an architect designs it and everyone is paid to build one part. A bazaar starts from a small seed: someone comes, then someone else, and no one knows in advance who will sell what or which relationships will form. In this member's view, government and much of today's work follow the cathedral model, and community change needs more of the bazaar mindset.Open in session

The fear of misusing power is now a greater risk than stepping in and actingWealth-building

One member working with community-led groups across Europe says local victories rarely travel across borders: governments make travel hard for Black and brown communities, and funding stays inside national lines. When partners first met online, the member could see their fear lift as they shared tactics. The member argues that being frozen by fear of a mistake is now more dangerous than stepping in and managing the risk, and asks how one local victory can grow into national and then regional change.Open in session

Systems-change models and generous leadership make catalytic capital go furtherCapital

Another member urges investors to read the systems-change models behind catalytic capital, such as the Water of Systems Change model and network theory, and to ask what leadership model a venture follows, since an ego-driven business cannot be catalytic. Some of the member's favourite investments are around $50,000: enough to get people together, write a report and put a stake in the ground.Open in session

A coalition of about 30 youth-led organisations plans to raise 10 million pounds together over three to five yearsA participant · Climate

Young leaders mapped their shared system as a forest and wrote one theory of change around outcomes rather than single organisations. A participant says the coalition is designed for co-founding from the start, built on trust between leaders, and that several co-founders run their groups in the evening after a day job. The first ask is 10 million pounds, shared among the members. Another participant adds that about 30 organisations already work together for free.Open in session

Small grants to small projects do not match a large problem, so funders and practitioners should plan togetherA member · Climate

A member points to the 30 young leaders who designed their collective in 24 hours of joint work. She argues that giving small amounts to small projects makes no sense for a big issue. A group of funders and a group of practitioners can write the theory of change and the strategy together, and build a model for the work in a short time.Open in session

Pooled funds let funders back partners they would not fund directly, and a youth circle helps decide where biodiversity money goesA member · Climate

A member describes one Synchronicity Earth pooled fund with 22 partners and 10 funders giving through it. Those funders would not give to the partners directly, but some do once they understand the work. Through the Chrysalis Youth Fund, a funding circle of young people advises on where biodiversity grants go.Open in session

High-impact networks share four principles: mission before organisation, trust not control, humility not brand, and constellations not stars.A member · Networks

A member finds the same leadership mindset across the high-impact networks she has studied for more than twenty years. People put the mission ahead of their organisation's self-interest and give up control when needed. They govern through trust, finding partners with shared values and then letting go. They share credit generously, which builds a reserve of goodwill for future collaboration. And they build constellations instead of little empires, because social change is complex, emergent and messy.Open in session

Network leaders nudge direction from behind and judge impact by their contribution instead of claiming credit.Networks

One member compares network leadership to "a cowboy at the back of the herd": the herd knows roughly where it is going, and the leader nudges it back on course now and then. Members say impact in networks should be shown as contribution rather than attribution, since relationships are hard to measure and system change often fails. They advise keeping at least one simple North Star metric, avoiding networks that exist only to convene, and collecting data in ways that strengthen the network.Open in session

Flying Labs puts local experts in charge in more than 35 countries, and the network's interdependence makes it resilient.A participant · Networks

A participant describes a network of local experts who own, decide on and lead the use of drones, data and geospatial AI in their own countries, and help to finance it. The central organisation stays small because its job is to bring people together, not to control them. Partners are neither dependent nor independent but interdependent, so when a funding shock hits one country, no single node is critical and other partners step in.Open in session

Clear, transparent boundaries let network partners hold each other to account without control from the top.A participant · Networks

Flying Labs keeps strengthening its network boundaries: transparent guidelines on what it means to be part of the network. Partners pay a small annual fee for access to shared resources and commit to the network's two values, sharing and collaboration. Each year partners assess themselves against those expectations. A participant finds that peers then hold each other accountable, which works better than oversight from the centre and lets the centre give up decision-making.Open in session

A campaign that hands the credit to its partners builds a broader coalition.Networks

One member describes an online safety campaign that built a wide coalition by giving smaller campaigns free help, including legal advice, and by sending journalists to speak to its grantees instead of to the funder. The member says the method has since been used by campaigns on social media regulation in other countries.Open in session

In South Wales, North Star Transition reframed river pollution as a question of how local businesses work.Networks

North Star Transition set up a Transition Lab that, by the account given in the room, brought together more than 200 stakeholders from farming, the environment, the NHS, energy and transport to decide what they want to change in their region. The lab's framing: "It's not about the rivers. It's about the business practice of people who live around the rivers." The network brought two development banks together, which set up a broad loan for farm transitions, and North Star has never claimed the credit.Open in session

AI and technology14 insights · 3 sessions
AI search and summaries threaten people's ability to check what was actually true.Information

One says access to frontier AI is subsidised by venture capital, so journalists and the public may lose it when prices rise. AI capability at one leading lab is improving about twice as fast as before, METR findsA participant · AI

A participant cites a recent METR report as finding that AI capability improved twice as fast over the past year as expected, mainly because existing models now write about 80% of the code for new ones. [METR's November 2026 assessment covers one lab, Anthropic. It estimates that the lab's models are improving at about twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025, and guesses that about 80% of that acceleration comes from the lab's use of AI in research and development. It gives no figure for the share of code written by AI.] He says this moves the field toward recursive self-improvement, where AI builds better AI around the clock, and that limits on compute and data centres are now less likely to slow development.Open in session

Donors anywhere can help start a tenfold increase in independent audits of frontier AI labsA member · AI

A member argues that where donors live does not limit where they can act, and much of the power over AI sits in the US. He says the labs are not transparent and that their most capable models are deployed internally, out of public view. He calls for at least ten times more third-party auditing inside the labs, which philanthropy can start, so that the public and politicians understand what these models can do.Open in session

Data centres make the harms of AI concrete for people todayAI

One member says data centres turn tech power into something everyone can see: emissions that put carbon targets out of reach, higher costs and pollution for nearby communities, the heaviest burden on marginalised communities, and questions about surveillance. Opposition to the build-out unites many movements at once. The same member points to competition policy and the EU Digital Markets Act as tools against present-day concentration of power.Open in session

Fewer data centres in the US slows dangerous AI, but middle powers still need compute of their ownA member · AI

A member holds both views at once. More data centres in the US means more capacity to train more dangerous models, so he wants fewer there. But he does not want the UK, Canada and other middle powers left without compute in an economy that runs on AI. Since the compute will be built somewhere, he would rather it go to democracies with clean energy than to authoritarian states.Open in session

Donors in AI safety have to choose trusted partners quickly and give at full size the first timeA member · AI

Philanthropy usually spends time mapping a field and making small learning grants. A member says AI does not allow that time: donors have to decide quickly whom to trust and write the right cheque to the right organisation the first time. Partner organisations report funding gaps of tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, and his fund spends each round of funding within three months instead of holding an endowment.Open in session

The line between today's AI harms and future AI risks is breaking downA participant · AI

A participant says the split between present harms and future risks no longer holds: surveillance infrastructure is being installed now, and AI may reach superhuman capability by the end of next year. Funders who focus on the highest-impact options, or find a trusted adviser, can make a large difference. "The future is not set in stone. There are many different paths that this could take. Some of them are really, really good paths."Open in session

The funder's role15 insights · 7 sessions
Funders can work backwards from the world they want in 15 years instead of trying to engineer outcomes.Framing the day

The hosts suggest that radical uncertainty calls for more than traditional philanthropy, where funders try to engineer outcomes and control the process toward them. Instead, members can picture the world they want in five, ten or fifteen years and work back to the most viable paths toward it. That also means offering resources that are not money, organising through aligned networks, and letting a new identity as changemakers emerge.Open in session

Funders can act as disruptors who change how money moves and as weavers who link communities.Priya Gupta · Framing the day

As disruptors, Priya Gupta says, funders challenge how money moves and who decides, and back the organising that changes the rules. As weavers, they pool, connect and link people in places, so that what emerges in one community can strengthen many. What is built in place shows what is possible, and organising changes the rules so that it can spread.Open in session

Place-based work lets funders share power, cross issue silos and see new models in practiceWealth-building

The facilitator gives three reasons Forward Global backs place-based work. Decisions about land, money, energy, housing and work are often made far from the people they affect, and philanthropy has repeated that pattern. Community leaders do not live single-issue lives, so working with them helps funders break out of climate, democracy and AI silos. And a real place shows new ways of being, with real people. Funders often dismiss such work as small, yet it adds up quickly.Open in session

Funders and communities build power together more easily when they acknowledge the power imbalance earlyA participant · Wealth-building

When Civic Power Fund began, it surveyed every community organisation it knew about its relationship with funders. A participant quotes one answer: "you think we're friends, but if I upset you, you won't fund me." He says naming the imbalance early makes it easier to build power together. Before him, another participant tells a story from Manchester: she asked two wealth holders in her own network for help, at some risk to herself, so that Rekindle could buy its building before a deadline.Open in session

The fear of misusing power is now a greater risk than stepping in and actingWealth-building

One member working with community-led groups across Europe says local victories rarely travel across borders: governments make travel hard for Black and brown communities, and funding stays inside national lines. When partners first met online, the member could see their fear lift as they shared tactics. The member argues that being frozen by fear of a mistake is now more dangerous than stepping in and managing the risk, and asks how one local victory can grow into national and then regional change.Open in session

Wealth holders should back a community owner for years after the purchase, and do it alongside othersA participant · Wealth-building

One member asks what Buy Back Brixton will need after the sale, when the hard work of running the market begins. A participant asks wealth holders to support the Brixton Traders and Community Association for a five-year period, to build the community's capacity to run it, and to do so with other funders rather than alone. She also asks for support beyond money: telling the story in rooms the community rarely gets into.Open in session

A funder should step back once others will fund the work without themA member · Capital

A member describes an additionality test: if someone else would give the million he is giving, "it's time to get off the bus". That takes discipline and setting ego aside, because the people funded no longer need you. On systems change, he adds that it has to be African money for African businesses.Open in session

Framing the dayForward Global

Gemma Mortensen↗

Framing the dayFounder, New Constellations · co-founder and Vice-Chair, More in Common

Gemma is a prize-winning social innovator and thinker. She co-founded More in Common, an international initiative to build more united and resilient societies, and is its Vice-Chair. She also founded New Constellations, which takes communities and institutions on journeys to imagine and move toward regenerative futures. She previously led Crisis Action, was Chief Global Officer at Change.org, and co-chaired a World Economic Forum council on systems leadership. She has also worked with the European Commission, the UN and as a journalist. She is a trustee of The HALO Trust and Bite Back 2030.

Since 2019 he has advised the impact investing business of Union Bancaire Privée, where he chairs the impact investment and biodiversity committees. He is active in venture capital for regenerative agriculture and food systems, as a general partner of Future Foodways and a member of Pymwymic's investment committee. He sits on the board of Toniic and is part of its 100% Network of investors committed to putting all their assets to work for impact. A CFA and Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, he supports conservation in Madagascar and recently moved back to the UK after many years in Switzerland.

Vanessa Sekhon

Vanessa is a performance strategist who coaches executives and teams using applied neuroscience and behavioural science. She developed the V4 Method™ while completing an MBA at the University of Oxford, focused on strategy, organisational behaviour and M&A. Her certifications include NLP Master Practitioner, applied neuroscience and brain health, accredited coach training (EMCC and AC), sleep and recovery coaching, HRV biofeedback and breath science. Her clients have included Amazon, HSBC, Bank of America and Audible.

William Perrin

Will works where technology, the state and the voluntary sector meet. In a long public-service career he helped set the UK's framework for regulating media, energy, gambling and licensing. As technology adviser to Prime Minister Tony Blair he managed the work that created Ofcom, and in 2007 he started the UK government's open data work. Later, his work with Professor Lorna Woods on a "duty of care" for online platforms underpinned the UK's Online Safety Act. He founded the community-journalism start-up Talk About Local, which won a Google Digital News Initiative award. He is a trustee of the Indigo Trust and Good Things Foundation, co-founded 360Giving, and is a long-time community activist in King's Cross. He convenes Forward Global members on the future of the information environment.

European Gathering 2026 › Main room

Framing the day: rupture and emergence

Sam Underwood · Melanie Ormos · Gemma Mortensen · Fernande Raine · Priya Gupta · Ruci Fixter · Amy Bray

  • Overview
  • Links14

What is breaking apart right now, and what is already emerging in its place?

The hosts open the third European Gathering with a frame taken from Canada's Prime Minister: this is a moment of rupture, not transition, and the next five years could shape the next five generations. Two short talks follow. Gemma Mortensen describes how rupture becomes real when it moves from the mind into the body, and what her gatherings keep returning to. Fernande Raine takes a historian's long view and finds beauty that grew out of earlier ruptures. After the table discussions, a second round of contributions begins with Priya Gupta, who calls scarcity an assumption, names the cost of living as the defining issue and points to communities taking ownership of wealth and power, with funders as disruptors and weavers. Ruci Fixter and Amy Bray close the round.

The hosts' frame: a moment of rupture, not transition

Sam Underwood, Melanie Ormos · Forward Global

The hosts open the day, which Forward Global holds in partnership with Pictet. They frame the day around rupture and emergence, and ask members to look beyond traditional philanthropy toward a long-range vision and the resources money alone cannot buy.

The day's frame is a moment of rupture, not a gradual transition.Rupture and emergence

The hosts take the theme from Canada's Prime Minister, Mark Carney, who said in January that the world is in a moment of rupture, not transition. They apply the idea to geopolitics, the environment, technology and culture at once: the world members took for granted is no longer a guide to what comes next. Their provocation for the day is that the next five years could shape the next five generations.

Every period of breakdown has produced people who built the alternative.Rupture and emergence

The hosts point to a pattern in history: in moments of rupture, individuals, collectives and communities take risks and make sacrifices to imagine, build, fund and invest in alternative systems, so that when breakdown comes there is something to turn to. They cite the National Health Service in the UK and the civil rights movements around the world, and ask members to see themselves as part of the next such story.

Funders can work backwards from the world they want in 15 years instead of trying to engineer outcomes.The funder's role · Rupture and emergence

The hosts suggest that radical uncertainty calls for more than traditional philanthropy, where funders try to engineer outcomes and control the process toward them. Instead, members can picture the world they want in five, ten or fifteen years and work back to the most viable paths toward it. That also means offering resources that are not money, organising through aligned networks, and letting a new identity as changemakers emerge.

When rupture becomes personal

Gemma Mortensen · Founder, New Constellations · co-founder and Vice-Chair, More in Common

Gemma Mortensen describes three moments when climate, AI and the collapse of democracy stopped being ideas and became felt. She explains how a year of questions about what we are living through led to New Constellations, and names the four themes every one of its groups returns to.

Rupture becomes real when it moves from the mind into the body.Gemma Mortensen · Rupture and emergence

Gemma Mortensen describes three moments when a crisis stopped being an idea for her. Climate became real when she saw her neighbours' children go to school in gas masks. AI became real when she read a pile of AI science fiction that her head of engineering gave her. The collapse of democracy became real with the assassination of a close friend by a right-wing white supremacist.

New Constellations grew out of people who could not go back to business as usual.Gemma Mortensen · Rupture and emergence · Networks and collaboration

After returning to the UK in 2019, Gemma Mortensen spent a year asking people what we are living through, what is breaking apart, what is emerging and how to live in times like these. Those questions became conversations, and the conversations became gatherings of people who also could not slot back into the status quo. New Constellations grew from those gatherings, taking communities and institutions on journeys toward regenerative futures.

Every New Constellations group returns to beauty, nature, love and the harm done by old systems.Gemma Mortensen · Rupture and emergence · Climate and nature

Across her gatherings, Gemma Mortensen hears the same themes: the transcendent beauty of a human life; the devastation that old systems of capital, power and technology have brought to the ability to live a simple human life; a profound wish to reinstate ourselves in the web of life and nature; and love in all its forms, from eros and philia to agape and philautia. One group of 24 young people made a candlelit artwork of the different kinds of love.

In their words4 quotes

A historian's view of emergence

Fernande Raine · Founder and CEO, The History Co:Lab

Fernande Raine steps back to a bird's eye view of history and finds that many social innovations grew out of rupture. She gives three examples, from the first Axial Age to the aftermath of the Second World War, and names two hopeful signals visible today: young people and collaborative networks.

A historian's long view shows that many social innovations grow out of rupture.Fernande Raine · Rupture and emergence

Fernande Raine says training as a historian teaches you to see the world from a bird's eye view, which also helps an entrepreneur. From that height she looks for patterns and signals of momentum for change. Over the longer arc of time, she finds, humans are able to do remarkable things, and many social innovations grow from rupture.

Rupture has produced beauty at least three times in recorded history.Fernande Raine · Rupture and emergence

Fernande Raine gives three examples. In the first Axial Age, between 800 and 200 BC, the weakening of tribal life as people connected more widely led to the first ideas of universal morality. After the Thirty Years' War, which she says cut Europe's population by a third [historians put the loss in the German lands, where most of the fighting took place, at between 15% and a third], she points to Baroque ceilings, Vivaldi, Galileo [who died in 1642, six years before the war ended], new navigation and the opening of new worlds. After the industrialised murder of the Second World War came institutions built to safeguard human dignity.

Two hopeful signals today are young people and networks that reject zero-sum thinking.Fernande Raine · Young leaders · Networks and collaboration

Fernande Raine sees two emergent principles. The first is young people full of hope, desire, love and creativity, and teaching that lets every child who dreams become who they imagine. The second is the power of networks that build communication and collaboration outside the zero-sum mindset. Her question for funders: what if we collaborated radically, with love, generosity and a sense of abundance?

In their words3 quotes

Place, community wealth and two roles for funders

Priya Gupta · Founding Trustee, Karillon Foundation · racial and gender justice activist

Priya Gupta, an economist, opens with the textbook definition of economics and calls scarcity an assumption. She describes an economy, places and systems that are all ruptured, with the cost of living as the defining issue. She sees a democratisation of wealth and power emerging, points to place-based work already represented among members, and asks funders to act as disruptors and weavers.

Scarcity is an assumption: the economy is a set of human choices, not a fixed law.Priya Gupta · Rupture and emergence · Capital and investment

Priya Gupta, an economist, recalls the first page of her first economics textbook: the study of the allocation of scarce resources. She calls all of it human construction. Scarcity is an assumption. Resources are a human definition that undervalues most people, nonhumans and the planet. Allocation is a set of human choices. Calling it a study, she says, hands collective power to something that seems beyond anyone's control.

The economy, places and political systems are all ruptured, and the cost of living is the defining issue.Priya Gupta · Rupture and emergence · Place and ownership

Priya Gupta names the cost of living as the defining issue of our time. Places are ruptured too: high streets are hollowed out and people's connection to place is broken. And systems are ruptured, with extreme wealth and power swaying whole democracies and fundamental rights and freedoms. She treats these as one rupture across the economy, place and power.

What is emerging is a democratisation of wealth and power, as communities move from being done to to being done with.Priya Gupta · Place and ownership · Capital and investment

Priya Gupta sees communities taking ownership of the decisions that shape their lives. She points to work already represented among members: a creative youth hub built as a permanent community asset, stewarded by and for young people; the campaign to bring Brixton Market into community ownership, as a matter of culture, belonging, health and democracy; a UK network of hubs reclaiming land, procurement, jobs and finance; a fund backing historically excluded communities; and wealth holders organising to rewire the tax system.

Funders can act as disruptors who change how money moves and as weavers who link communities.Priya Gupta · The funder's role · Networks and collaboration

As disruptors, Priya Gupta says, funders challenge how money moves and who decides, and back the organising that changes the rules. As weavers, they pool, connect and link people in places, so that what emerges in one community can strengthen many. What is built in place shows what is possible, and organising changes the rules so that it can spread.

Organisations and projects

  • Forward Global · The hosts: Forward Global is the community of more than 300 wealth stewards that convenes the European Gathering.
  • Pictet philanthropy services · The hosts: Pictet, whose advisers help families and foundations plan their giving, is Forward Global's partner for the day.
  • New Constellations · Gemma Mortensen: the initiative she founded takes communities and institutions on journeys of reflection toward regenerative futures, and its gatherings are the source of the four themes in her talk.
  • More in Common · Gemma Mortensen: the international initiative she co-founded studies the forces that drive societies apart and works to show what people still share.
  • The History Co:Lab · Fernande Raine: the civic innovation lab she leads works with schools, museums and archives so that young people grow up ready to take part in democracy.
  • Buy Back Brixton · Priya Gupta: the campaign to bring Brixton's markets into community ownership is her example of ownership as a matter of culture, belonging, health and democracy.

Reports and data

  • JRF cost of living tracker, summer 2026 · Priya Gupta: the Joseph Rowntree Foundation's regular survey of low-income households puts numbers on the cost of living pressure she calls the defining issue of our time.

Law and policy

  • National Health Service Act 1946 · The hosts: this is the Act that founded the NHS, which they cite as an alternative system built by people who took risks in a time of rupture.
  • Universal Declaration of Human Rights · Fernande Raine: the 1948 declaration belongs to the post-war effort to build institutions that safeguard human dignity, her third example of what can follow a rupture.

Books and ideas

  • Mark Carney, "Principled and pragmatic: Canada's path" · The hosts: the Canadian Prime Minister's speech to the World Economic Forum on 20 January 2026 is the source of the day's frame, where he says the world is in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.
  • Axial Age · Fernande Raine: the philosopher Karl Jaspers gave this name to the centuries around 800 to 200 BC, when new philosophies and ideas of universal morality arose in several civilisations.
  • Thirty Years' War · Fernande Raine: the European war of 1618 to 1648 is her second example of a rupture that was followed by new art, science and exploration.
  • Community wealth building · Priya Gupta: the Centre for Local Economic Strategies explains the approach to local economies behind her talk, in which wealth is owned more democratically and kept circulating locally.

Further reading

  • Trust the process: the story of New Constellations · Gemma Mortensen: Caroline McGinn tells how New Constellations began and what its journeys ask of the people who join them.

Community Wealth-Building

  • Overview
  • Transcript
  • Links19

What does it take for a community to own the places it depends on?

A Forward Global facilitator opens with three reasons to fund in place: power, issue silos and the chance to show new models with real people. A participant tells the story of Buy Back Brixton, the traders' campaign to bring Brixton Market into community ownership after years under private equity. A second participant describes community organising that grows from one victory to the next, from school uniform rules in Brixton to a disability organisation in Warwickshire and a sick pay campaign for cleaners. A third participant argues for treating such projects as system demonstrators. Questions turn to the power money holds, and the hour closes on what funders can do after the purchase.

Insights 12

Place-based work lets funders share power, cross issue silos and see new models in practicePlace and ownership · The funder's role

The facilitator gives three reasons Forward Global backs place-based work. Decisions about land, money, energy, housing and work are often made far from the people they affect, and philanthropy has repeated that pattern. Community leaders do not live single-issue lives, so working with them helps funders break out of climate, democracy and AI silos. And a real place shows new ways of being, with real people. Funders often dismiss such work as small, yet it adds up quickly.04:43

Brixton Market's value comes from its culture, and private equity owners extract that valueA participant · Place and ownership · Capital and investment

A participant says modern Brixton took shape after 1948, when people who arrived from the Caribbean on the Windrush settled there and called it home. He says its market, nearly 100 years old, has about 170 small traders and some 200 languages. A private equity firm bought it in 2018. Since then independent shops have given way to chains, and each new private equity owner, he says, raises rents and service charges by about 20%. The building is worth more "because it's Brixton."08:17

Brixton's traders organised to stop their market going to another private equity firmA participant · Place and ownership

A participant says that when the market came up for sale, a trader of 15 years drew a line: it must not go to another private equity firm. With wealth holders and groups including the Good Ancestor Movement behind them, the traders made a competitive offer. Lambeth Council listed the site as an Asset of Community Value in July 2026, which made a quick sale harder. In September 2026 the campaign was named preferred buyer, and it is still raising funds.09:25

Community ownership changes the question from what rent justifies the valuation to who needs the spaceA participant · Place and ownership

A participant says the buyer, the Brixton Traders and Community Association, has recently been incorporated as a charitable community benefit society. Every member has one vote, and its board of 12 will have four or five traders, with the wider community in the majority. He says private owners ask what a space must earn to justify the valuation, while a community owner asks who is missing a space and how to fill it. The association will answer to "the people we see daily."47:57

In community organising, one local victory inspires the nextA participant · Place and ownership

A participant follows a chain of wins. He says young women in Brixton formed the Halo campaign and changed their school's uniform rules on Afro hair; the Halo Code that came out of it is a pledge that schools and workplaces across the UK have signed. Some went on to help start Buy Back Brixton. In Coventry and Warwickshire, he says, the community around Grapevine, a disability group that grew out of family-run discos, turned out the day after Warwickshire's Reform-led county council cut disability spending, and the council backed down within a week. He says that group is now buying a building.13:11

Community organisers listen first and let the issue come from the people they listen toA participant · Place and ownership

A participant says community organising starts by listening, never by choosing the issue. He describes an organiser who ran listening campaigns with South American cleaners in the UK. After COVID, the cleaners' deepest fear was falling sick and losing their income, and that fear became the Safe Sick Pay campaign, which he says has since won two of its four demands and safer sick pay for millions of people in the UK. His rule: "The people you listen to are the people you train to become leaders."49:41

Funders should treat community projects as system demonstrators for the next economyA participant · Place and ownership · Capital and investment

A participant says the Good Ancestor Movement asks wealthy individuals, families and institutions to move capital from extraction toward a regenerative economy, because much institutional philanthropy is too slow or unfit for this work. She sees Buy Back Brixton as a test of relocalising production and consumption in a community that is already organised. Such work, she says, should be seen as system demonstrators and not as "cute community projects", alongside CIVIC SQUARE in Birmingham and community energy rooted in place.19:47

Funders and communities build power together more easily when they acknowledge the power imbalance earlyA participant · The funder's role

When Civic Power Fund began, it surveyed every community organisation it knew about its relationship with funders. A participant quotes one answer: "you think we're friends, but if I upset you, you won't fund me." He says naming the imbalance early makes it easier to build power together. Before him, another participant tells a story from Manchester: she asked two wealth holders in her own network for help, at some risk to herself, so that Rekindle could buy its building before a deadline.36:16

Community change grows like a bazaar, while governments plan like cathedral buildersNetworks and collaboration · Place and ownership

One member contrasts two approaches. A cathedral is planned from the top: an architect designs it and everyone is paid to build one part. A bazaar starts from a small seed: someone comes, then someone else, and no one knows in advance who will sell what or which relationships will form. In this member's view, government and much of today's work follow the cathedral model, and community change needs more of the bazaar mindset.40:32

Brixton's market traders already link London to producers in AfricaA participant · Place and ownership

One funder taking part says their foundation backs livelihood programmes in Africa that sell to export markets, yet had never connected that work to London. Another participant says the link was not obvious to him either, until a trader in Brixton Village told him most of his products come from Africa, some of them his own. Every morning, he says, a shipment from Africa supplies Brixton's small traders, and that link should be part of how funders support communities globally.39:48

The fear of misusing power is now a greater risk than stepping in and actingThe funder's role · Networks and collaboration

One member working with community-led groups across Europe says local victories rarely travel across borders: governments make travel hard for Black and brown communities, and funding stays inside national lines. When partners first met online, the member could see their fear lift as they shared tactics. The member argues that being frozen by fear of a mistake is now more dangerous than stepping in and managing the risk, and asks how one local victory can grow into national and then regional change.44:04

Wealth holders should back a community owner for years after the purchase, and do it alongside othersA participant · The funder's role · Place and ownership

One member asks what Buy Back Brixton will need after the sale, when the hard work of running the market begins. A participant asks wealth holders to support the Brixton Traders and Community Association for a five-year period, to build the community's capacity to run it, and to do so with other funders rather than alone. She also asks for support beyond money: telling the story in rooms the community rarely gets into.53:40

Facilitator:Amazing. Thank you, everybody, and thank you for joining this session, which we've been really excited about. Facilitator:Three reasons I think are important to emphasise. One is this question of power. We know that philanthropy, and at times public service provision, has perpetuated those same dynamics, and it's very hard, maybe even impossible, to get around that without working in place and with community leaders. Facilitator:The second is it helps break down silos. Participant A:It's such a moment, sometimes it's difficult to know where to start and how to frame it. But I think for those of you that don't, who doesn't know Brixton as a place? Just a few people. This was the only place that invited them, and they called it home.06:22

Participant A:And there was a market there then, which next year will be 100 years old, and London was filled with markets at that time. This was sort of a market built during the 30s. Participant A:And I'm from Brixton, I've lived there my whole life, and the market was acquired in 2018 by a private equity firm for [figures omitted], and that changed our community quite drastically. Participant A:And so about a year ago, we as traders came together and decided to stand together, to support each other and to stop this disruption, this extraction and this monetisation of our cultural capital that we have created. Participant A:And so, through that process, they put it on the market three months ago [the campaign's timeline dates the sale process to September 2024 and the community bid to June 2026]. Participant A:And so we came together and made an offer, a very competitive offer, through the support of all these angels, as we call them now, wealth generators, the likes of the Good Ancestor Movement and a few other organisations. Participant B:During Covid they went online, they grew, and for years they just invested in their community and talking to their neighbours. Participant B:These are all people who had voted Reform. They had voted these people into power. [They] turned up the next day and said, oh no, no, we won't take that. Participant 3:Can I ask a little bit more about how [the ownership model] works? How does it work with the members and the traders who are there already? Maybe can you speak more about the community?26:30

Participant A:Yeah, it's actually really simple. We've recently been incorporated as a charitable community benefit society, so it's a membership model. It's called the Brixton Traders and Community Association. So it's part trader representative members, and then the wider [community]. We have a forum that is majority community, minority traders, and then we have a membership that is also majority community, minority traders.26:49

Participant A:But we recognise that the traders are at the heart. They are nodes for the community, so we have to empower them so that they can support the community.27:15

Participant 3:And then on the decision making, it's a member organisation?27:26

Participant A:Correct, yes, it's a membership organisation. And so every member will have a single vote, and the board will be a board of 12, of which four or five will be traders and the rest will be the wider community.27:29

Participant 4:I hadn't heard about the initiative until [a member of the Forward Global team] waxed lyrical about how amazing it was, and it really is incredible and super inspiring. And I think, as you were saying, the catalytic effect of this will be [that] other people here, not just other communities but wealth holders, can also be inspired by what is possible and help to support that type of initiative. Because community, in the world we're in now, is more important than ever.27:44

Participant A:I would say, on the community point, something interesting happened recently. I went on national TV, French national TV, in Brixton, and I landed in Paris and three people pointed me out. It blew my mind.28:40

Participant A:I met the CEO of the service organisation that manages Brixton Market. He was responsible for 25 shopping centres around the country. And he said, [participant], I've spent the last 30 years ripping out markets around the country, and I've realised how much damage that's done. Even the shopping centres now can't sustain, because the model isn't a shopping centre. The market represents something way more than what we thought it was.28:54

Participant A:And actually these investors coming in and replacing our markets with shopping centres has done huge damage to our country. And so he got it instinctively, and he recognised that it is about that.29:23

Participant A:And actually I was talking to [a member], who said they were supporting [work in parts of Africa], and had a thought about the fact that, speaking to the traders in Brixton, nearly all the traders are making products from somewhere else instead of here. So we are completely connected in a global sense, and supporting so many other ecosystems because of that.29:39

Participant A:And so our markets are so much more than a simple trade that Amazon can kill. You can't kill a community, you can't kill a market. So there's something we're protecting that we need to define. I think we just feel it. We feel it now. We have to study it, and we have to be able to articulate it so we can bring all of this back.30:04

30:36On the power that money holds

Participant 5:Thank you so much for sharing all of your examples. I've been documenting examples, making the business case for why working in deep trust, authentic relationships, human to human, fostering community, is [what creates] change. So that [could] be helpful in supporting your work, so people don't see it as a cute project, but rather the most effective way to achieve transformational change.30:36

Participant 6:I'm trying to decide whether to ask my question, but I think I will. I've been thinking a lot about circling back to the question of power and power dynamics, and the power over, as you mentioned, but more deeply the power that comes with funding and wealth holders, even those that are well-intentioned and want to do good. And I wondered if, I don't want to put anyone on the spot, but if there's any lessons learned from the work that you've done with funders that is useful for other funders and wealth holders to know and think about, to better look at the power that money holds?31:18

Participant C:So, I don't know if this is going to answer your question, but I just feel the need to presence this in the room, because I alluded to the fact that there are many co-conspirators here. And two of our beloved community from the Good Ancestor Movement are [here]. And as an individual running an organisation that has folks like them as key stakeholders, because we're trying to mobilise them towards a particular practice of redistribution, there is an inherent power dynamic, right?32:17

Participant C:I think it was a year ago, I can't remember, there was a capital campaign that wasn't even called a capital campaign at the time. There was a movement partner of ours that does fantastic work up in Manchester. They run a critical thinking club for working-class kids. Black-led, extraordinary work, extraordinary leadership. And at the time, everything in the organisation wasn't neat, it wasn't clearly defined.32:59

Participant C:We're very anxious about power as well, and how we steward our power as an organisation that develops relationships with communities and movements and wealth holders. So bringing those who have resources together with those who need resources, and navigating that tightrope. And I didn't know what to do, because this organisation had a time-limited opportunity to purchase their building from their landlord, right, and they had a gap.33:30

Participant C:And I just thought, I can't say no to this opportunity to galvanise folks around this opportunity that the organisation had. But I need help. And so who did I call? [Those two members], right? To feel risk, to deepen relationship, by trusting people that I could choose to see as having power over me, and actually just entering a place of vulnerability. And beyond that actually, the collective strategy and the collective intelligence between us that emerged.34:00

Participant C:And then we rolled out this capital campaign. Rekindle School got their building, and it was multiple exchanges of trust. I share that because I don't want to roll out a really theoretical example. I want to talk to you about my practice and what it takes to build that collective power.34:45

Participant C:I'm glad this has come back around, because I did an organising training a couple of years ago, and the first thing we learned was power is the ability to act. And we're going to need a lot more of that power. And if I had shrunk in my corner and stood on, should I do this or not, we wouldn't have started this [inaudible] of moving resources towards communities and building power collectively across the ecosystem.35:12

Participant C:Obviously [those two members] have a particular orientation to power that is different and distinctive, but we can have those conversations. And that's not something that comes naturally to anyone. It has to be learning, it has to be a practice. So I just encourage you to lean into that practice.35:45

Participant B:And it's always going to feel risky, right? When we first [started Civic Power Fund], the first thing we did for the first couple of months, we sent a survey out to every [community organisation] we knew, asking about their relationship with [funders]. And I remember one bit of feedback that was really going to stay with me. Someone wrote down: you think we're friends, but if I upset you, you won't fund me.36:16

Participant B:And I think for me that was just such a brutal, immediate reminder that there is power in that relationship. And if you don't acknowledge that power, if you don't turn around and say, yeah, we aren't actually always on the same playing field, right, there is an imbalance between us. But if we can acknowledge that really early on, then we can build power together much easier. I think it's when we avoid it, when we feel awkward about something.37:02

Participant B:But the liberation is when you actually turn around and you're like, I do have that power and I'm going to use it. And I'm going to use it for the benefit [of] something that I believe in. And that only comes through dialogue.37:37

37:49On trade links and solidarity across borders

Facilitator:I see four questions, so I want to maybe do two rounds of two, and then we have about ten minutes left. We want to make sure we have a bit of time for very practically what people can do to help.37:49

Participant 7:My question was very simple, and it's already been asked, so I'll just use my time to endorse what [a participant] was saying. Just to throw out there a bit of vulnerability-sharing: as a foundation, we support a lot of work in [parts of Africa], and there we do livelihood programmes, and part of that is selling to export markets. And I saw the world as different. Here it is in London, UK, and that's over there, and we do that over there because it's in need.38:07

Participant 7:And we do this great project because it makes sense, because you connect to export markets, and then just didn't connect the final step. Then here you have a cultural hub like London, Brixton, that final step. So seeing global communities not just as communities of practice, but actually linked through things like trade and commerce. Those are the systems that we sought to leverage, but just didn't go all the way to connect the dots here. So thank you for pointing out the obvious.38:44

Participant A:And I have to put my hands up and say that wasn't obvious to me too. I think that realisation came to fruition as we were discussing this. And I was talking to some of the traders yesterday, one particularly, a trader who has a small spot in Brixton Village, and he's thriving, he's selling so many coconuts, right? And most of his products are from Africa.39:16

Participant A:And I said to him, so how are you thinking about growing this? And he said, of course, I have my own products in Africa. That's what's coming across. And then it dawned on me, this is just yesterday, that every morning I get to Brixton, there is a shipment from Africa on which most of the stuff being sold in Brixton by small traders [arrives], and that's the connection. That's 179 shops, right? From the fashion to the food, to the clothing, all of it.39:48

Participant A:So I think that it's a big realisation for me too, that this should be part of the vision of how we support globally.40:15

Facilitator:Thank you. Let's take these three comments before we turn it back. We'll do the three at once.40:25

Participant 8:Yeah, thanks so much for sharing. So we're talking about the market, and [there is an analogy I use,] the bazaar approach. And it's like, we're going to start, someone's going to come, we don't know what we're going to do, someone else will come, and eventually you build a market, a bazaar, from that. You don't know what that's going to look like, you don't know who's going to sell what, or who's going to come, or what the relationships are going to be, but we need to start with that little seed.40:32

Participant 8:And we contrast that with the cathedral approach, which is: we've got a plan for this big cathedral, we know where everyone needs to go, the architect designed it, everyone's been paid to do this little bit of it, and together we create a cathedral. And I think a lot of the work that's been done today is the cathedral approach, and very top down as well. The government has the cathedral mindset, and we want to bring more of a bazaar mindset.40:57

Participant 8:So with that sort of analogy in mind, what can you share with the group that is about bringing that bazaar mindset not just to the Brixton market, but to everything that people do? Because it's so applicable.41:22

Facilitator:I'll take two more before we jump in. But quickly on that, there is one of the working groups afterwards on network principles and practice, going deeper on this, so for those who want to learn more, that would be a good one to go to.41:38

Participant 9:Well, lots of things are coming up. But the one was around how you were talking about one community victory that inspired another victory, another victory, and I'm finding that to be one of the cases of hope. I don't want to be cliché, but the work that we're doing is in these very community-driven, community-led, community-focused areas across Europe.41:51

Participant 9:And one of the struggles is around building these, almost, highways of solidarity, as I call it. It's so hard to make those connections, because it's so hard to cross borders, for one, if governments make it increasingly difficult, especially for black and brown communities, to get passports and cross borders in meaningful ways. Secondly, funding is very localised as well. It's either very UK focused, or Germany, or US, whatever, and [not] this kind of cross-regional support to enable these highways of solidarity to come into being.42:25

Participant 9:We had an online call where we brought our partners together. It was the first time. Participant 9:And it's not a question we have to answer now, but it is about how do you inspire one community's local victory into something that transcends into something that's national, into something that's regional. Participant 9:And then the thing around power. I think the fear of how you're going to use that power is more debilitating and higher risk than actually just stepping into it and saying, let's do the thing, and let's see how we can mitigate for it. 44:55On running the market after the purchase

Participant 10:I just wanted to add my praise for Rekindle, because it is amazing. So I wanted to ask you a question about how you deal with what must be a feeling of such intense responsibility. It's one thing to pull off buying, that's huge, right? But with that, you're doing things first, and you know everyone's watching. There's a whole load of people [inaudible], and then there's a whole load of people who are just watching to see what happens.44:55

Participant 10:And the hard stuff, doesn't it come after that? It comes when you've got it, and you're responsible for it. And I just wonder how you're dealing with that, but also what do you need? Because it's amazing what you've done to rally the capital around, and it's going to happen, clearly you're going to do it, no doubt. But then what do you need? Because it feels like there's a collective responsibility to invest in that too.45:25

Participant A:I thought your question was really something that we've been thinking a lot about. There's an initiative that I did separately to Buy Back Brixton, which was to sign an agreement between Amsterdam Southeast and Brixton. Amsterdam Southeast is very similar to Brixton in many, many ways, and it's a very similar community. And two weeks ago, 150 of them travelled to Brixton, and I had our mayor there, our head of council there and all our community leaders, and we signed an agreement to share ideas.45:58

Participant A:And I travelled to Amsterdam myself to understand how they navigated this, and they approached this in a very similar way. They have an organisation that raised quite a lot of money to buy streets parallel to the red light district, and they bought a couple of hundred of those buildings. So they've been thinking a lot about how communities are represented and how they switch the power of how these assets are allocated. I found that so, so fascinating.46:31

Participant A:And that sort of leads to the economics that [we heard about this morning]. This is really about how we're thinking about who should have access to those assets, right? And I think when that's democratised, when that is not on my shoulders, I'm not going to make that decision. That's a board that represents the wider community, that's membership, that's all looking at how we're making these decisions. I think that allows the talent in the community, from the ground up, to fill the spaces that our community needs.47:06

Participant A:And actually that solves a huge problem with empty spaces. Because what happens when you start from the top down is it's all through the current economic models: how much is this going to generate, so that we can justify the valuation? But now, it's not about that. We're thinking about, OK, how do we fill the space? How do we ensure that someone who is missing that space gets that space? So it's completely different economics, and I think that's what we get to define.47:57

Participant A:Just coming back to your point, I think we learn that through these international coalitions. On your question, the weight on our shoulders: we're the five board members right now, we're recruiting the additional seven, and we feel that. And I think The Advocacy Academy have done a great job in the campaign and in getting attention.48:23

Participant A:What we as board members, as community leaders, have been thinking mostly about is, in many ways we were assuming that acquisition would happen, and we're just worried about: what does it look like? How does it change? What is the new economics, and how do we justify it to our community? Because that's [who] we will be held accountable [to]. It won't be a bank or any private equity firm. It will be the people we see daily.49:03

Participant A:So how do you balance that? I don't know. What we need is a structure. So I can share that with anyone else that needs to read that.49:30

Participant B:[We do] community organising. It's a practice, it's a methodology. And the start of that methodology effectively says: if you are working with a community, you don't go in and decide the issue, you listen first for the issue.49:41

Participant B:So we found a wonderful woman, [an organiser], and her family were South American, and she worked with a lot of South American cleaners. She ran a big listening campaign for South American cleaners, and it turned into various campaigns at different quarters around the UK, where the cleaners were going to strike [inaudible]. She won a lot of victories.50:05

Participant B:And then she travelled to the US on a scholarship and met people who were running cleaning campaigns in the US, and she came back completely different and was like, I'm not fighting small battles anymore. And she ran another listening campaign, and basically spent a long time talking to cleaners about what was really the pain in their life. This was not too long after COVID, and I think [what] came out [was] sick pay. [The cleaners] had a genuine fear that [they would] catch COVID-19 when they were cleaning people's houses, getting sick and losing their income.50:33

Participant B:And [she] worked really methodically, slowly, and built an organisation called Safe Sick Pay that had four demands. They won two of those demands, and they have now won safe sick pay for 10 million people in the UK [the campaign and the TUC estimate that more than 7 million workers gain from sick pay from day one]. And we all asked her that question: what are you going to do now with all eyes on you? And she was like, if I had had this many eyes on me at the start, I would have won all four.51:11

Participant B:And I think there's that thing of, these things grow from really small seeds into big ideas. Small local campaigns about wages don't immediately seem like mass change. But nothing does.51:43

Participant B:But I think what we always say is, [in organising], you listen to people and you develop their ability to lead. The people you listen to are the people you train to become leaders. That is the core principle. You do not know what is coming. What [she] has built is an institution that will stand for a long time, that will serve a lot of people. And I think for us that's the methodology. Just go where the energy is, and give them money.52:09

52:47On what a funder can do next

The easiest thing is to speak to people in the room over lunch, get to know the work a little bit more. Come speak to us if you'd like connections; we can help you navigate the space.52:47

Facilitator:But maybe let's imagine two different fictional people. What sort of easy buttons, to use an American term, exist, where there is an existing infrastructure that they can just support?53:09

Participant C:[Buy Back Brixton is] the perfect example of both the easy button and championing a cause, really getting engaged. So the beautiful thing about [this] is that we get to use all forms of our capital. And so if you're ready to deploy financial capital, then to your point about what happens on day two, I would love it if you would join me in supporting the Brixton Traders and Community Association for a five-year period. Because we need to back you not just on day one.53:40

Participant C:Because to your point, this is about: what does this look like? How do we build the capacity within communities to steward that beyond this thing? So there is an opportunity to do that, and [you] should of course talk to the experts, but I would love to travel alongside other wealth holders. Because I think the other thing about this is it can be very limiting if you're moving in this way that deeply shifts power by yourself. That is why I never try to do anything by myself.54:27

Participant C:So that's the kind of thing that we've heard from other organisations, Power to Prosper, [Civic] Power Fund. All this work exists, and I think our role is to back it, and back it using all forms of capital that we have.54:55

Participant C:And one more thing: beyond being disruptive in the way we [use] capital, it's also going out to the spaces where you occupy those rooms that folks sometimes don't get to be in, and being able to tell the story, deeply rooted in what we've heard about what we're imagining, not just about what came before, but what might be possible. So now everybody's beautifully equipped, and I would encourage us to be brave and go out there and be able to tell a story.55:13

Facilitator:Beautifully said. Thank you. Anyone else like to add on that?55:53

Participant 11:For Buy Back Brixton, I know there's a lot happening for us to come to support as well. There's the December 4th fundraiser event. I would definitely be going to that.55:59

Facilitator:Wonderful. It's such an important point. We often hear the same: especially in this moment, a lot of Forward Global members say, I don't want to do this alone, it feels overwhelming. And I think because this work is so relational, so collaborative in its DNA, we find people find a lot of joy in the work.56:20

Participant 12:Power to Prosper is a great example. [inaudible] People like Power to Prosper show us the networks that [this is] happening with.56:38

Facilitator:Yeah, totally. So if there are other places close to your heart, in different parts of the UK or the world, I'm sure we can find movements like this to support. We are about out of time; we're going to go to lunch. Thank you so much for speaking.57:10

Facilitator:Thank you so much for being part of this.
