It has to wait to see the [next] lily pad, so it can jump onto the alternative. And that's what you're all building. So if we can fund that and resource that, I think that would be a beautiful thing to do. Enjoy lunch.57:53

Organisations and projects

  • Buy Back Brixton · The campaign by traders and residents to bring Brixton Village and Market Row into community ownership, which a participant describes.
  • Civic Power Fund · The UK's first pooled fund dedicated to community organising, which backs the groups in a participant's stories.
  • Good Ancestor Movement · An organisation that works with wealthy individuals and their advisers to move wealth towards a regenerative economy.
  • CIVIC SQUARE · A Birmingham organisation that demonstrates neighbourhood-scale civic infrastructure for the climate transition, which a participant names as a system demonstrator.
  • The Advocacy Academy · The Brixton youth organising charity whose young members form the Halo Collective and work with the traders on the campaign.
  • The Halo Collective · The alliance of young Black organisers behind the Halo Code, which asks schools and workplaces to end discrimination against Afro hair.
  • Grapevine Coventry and Warwickshire · The charity whose long work with disabled people and their families a participant describes as slow power.
  • Safe Sick Pay campaign · The Centre for Progressive Change campaign for sick pay from the first day of illness, which a participant traces back to listening campaigns with cleaners.
  • Rekindle School · A youth-led supplementary school for working-class young people in Manchester, which a participant's network helps to buy its building.

Reports and data

  • Resourcing the Solidarity Economy · The report by Decolonising Economics with the Good Ancestor Movement that a participant recommends as the way into this work.

Law and policy

  • Brixton Village listed as an Asset of Community Value · Lambeth Council's announcement that Brixton Village and Market Row are on its list of assets of community value, which gives the community time to prepare a bid when the site is put up for sale.
  • Community Right to Buy · Locality explains the new right in the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act, which gives community groups first refusal on listed assets and 12 months to raise the money.
  • Co-operative and Community Benefit Societies Act 2014 · The Financial Conduct Authority's guide to the law behind community benefit societies, the legal form the Brixton Traders and Community Association uses.
  • Statutory Sick Pay from day one · The government's announcement that employees receive sick pay from the first day of illness from April 2026, the reform the Safe Sick Pay campaign pressed for.

Books and ideas

  • The Cathedral and the Bazaar · Eric S. Raymond's essay on planned and open ways of building software made this contrast famous, and the session applies the same contrast to community change.
  • History of the Empire Windrush · Royal Museums Greenwich tells the story of the ship that brought Caribbean passengers to Britain in 1948, the arrival a participant places at the start of modern Brixton.
  • What is community organising? · A plain introduction from Community Organisers to the practice a participant describes, which begins with reaching out and listening.

Further reading

  • Keys to the future: How we build a new era of community ownership · A 2026 report by Locality and Power to Change that sets out what government and funders can do to help more communities own the places they depend on.
  • Funding Justice 3 · Civic Power Fund's analysis of more than 20,000 UK social justice grants, which tracks how much of that money reaches community organising.

To learn more or engage further on this topic, please reach out to Sam Underwood or Melanie Ormos.

European Gathering 2026 › Working group

Catalytic capital: the whole spectrum of capital for systems change

  • Overview
  • Transcript
  • Links18

How can funders use every kind of capital, from grants to investment, to change systems?

Four contributors set out how grants, catalytic capital and investment can work together for systems change. The recording starts after the first two openings, from a participant and a member, which were not recorded. A second participant describes starting from values, and a third describes how each kind of capital clears a different barrier. One member argues that strong returns do not change a system on their own and that catalytic capital has to fund the uncertain early stages. The discussion turns to stepping back when others will fund, keeping finance local in Africa, and how far wealth holders will accept lower returns.

Insights 10

Stating your values first lets you apply them to both giving and investingA participant · Capital and investment

A participant says being intentional with capital is hard, because it is hard to know what matters to you. Tribe Impact Capital built its Impact DNA process, which uses the UN Sustainable Development Goals to help clients articulate their values. Once those values are clear, they become a golden thread for applying capital across the whole spectrum, whether that is giving or investing.01:52

Catalytic capital is the unglamorous work of building systemsA participant · Capital and investment

A participant does not love the term catalytic capital, because she thinks all capital should work this way. For her it means "the less sexy stuff": the systems. She asks members to put capital where they might not see immediate outcomes, where it can build consensus and support the systems that let more good work happen, including a stronger impact ecosystem in the UK.02:44

Impact investing is an approach that applies across every assetA participant · Capital and investment

A participant says each kind of capital knocks down a different barrier. Philanthropy can fund policy work, catalytic capital de-risks deals to attract mainstream money, and a family office with an operating business can act directly. His one takeaway: impact investing is an approach "that you can have across all of the assets". He adds that the UK impact investing market is growing.06:03

UK foundations are slightly ahead of family offices in aligning their grants and investmentsA participant · Capital and investment

A participant finds that UK foundations are slightly further ahead than families in trying to make their grant-making and their investment portfolios congruent, though some family offices are far ahead. Foundations are also more public, so their experience is easier to learn from. Family wealth is private and complex, which is why he sees peer communities of funders as valuable.08:19

A portfolio can perform well for 20 years without changing the system around itCapital and investment

One member describes a long record in impact investing with almost no losses. Those investments did great things, but they did not change the system. Working with hundreds of local stakeholders, the member's team has distilled a long list of interventions into a few packages, yet no one has funded the slow work of originating the investments that could follow.10:06

Catalytic capital is needed before anyone can say what the deal isCapital and investment

The same member says investors ask what the deal is and what the benefits will be, when at the start nobody knows. Large funders compete to fund the problem on the front page and ignore deeper causes. Catalytic capital has different roles at each stage: bringing disconnected stakeholders together, originating investments, building the mechanisms for investing, and the structures that combine finance, technology, skills and knowledge.13:23

Systems-change models and generous leadership make catalytic capital go furtherCapital and investment · Networks and collaboration

Another member urges investors to read the systems-change models behind catalytic capital, such as the Water of Systems Change model and network theory, and to ask what leadership model a venture follows, since an ego-driven business cannot be catalytic. Some of the member's favourite investments are around $50,000: enough to get people together, write a report and put a stake in the ground.15:26

A funder should step back once others will fund the work without themA member · The funder's role · Capital and investment

A member describes an additionality test: if someone else would give the million he is giving, "it's time to get off the bus". That takes discipline and setting ego aside, because the people funded no longer need you. On systems change, he adds that it has to be African money for African businesses.19:55

An impact investor with a mainstream investor's mindset changes very littleA participant · Capital and investment

A participant says anyone who works on entrenched issues and is curious, genuine and low-ego ends up thinking about systems, because their money is a drop in the ocean. Access works to bring money into markets nobody wants to fund, packaged so foundations take an interest. She says "there is no point in being an impact investor with the mindset of a mainstream investor", because unless behaviours and incentives change, impact becomes a product to sell.22:49

Treating wealth as excess money that does not need to grow makes lower returns acceptableCapital and investment

One member names the mental hurdle of accepting 3% for solar panels on schools when an index fund returns about 7%. Once wealth holders see their money as already excess, with no need to grow, accepting 2 or 3% and doing a lot with it becomes exciting. Another member asks where the midpoint sits between concessionary and market-rate capital, since the concessionary pool is small.24:24

00:14On values and intentional capital

Facilitator:Can you talk to me about your clients and how they can [put] impact first, and their goals, and then what are the tools that they can use?00:14

Participant A:Sure. I just wanted to talk about two things. The first is this piece of the intentionality, which I think is really important. The second is a comment on the system, and I will come to that in a second.00:25

Participant A:As I start out, I'm very visual. When I think about capital, I literally think about one of those whole semicircles. Participant A:My undergraduate dissertation was on philanthropy [inaudible], and that was the start of [it]. Participant A:And we believe that a really useful way of doing that is through the narrative of sustainability. Participant A:We have [inaudible] part of building a kind of greater and stronger resilience system in the impact space in the UK. And we are still tiny, but that is something that we're quite proud of and we want to keep building together.03:13

Organisations and projects

  • Tribe Impact Capital · A UK impact wealth manager that builds portfolios around each client's values.
  • Impact Investing Institute · The UK's independent body for growing impact investing.
  • Access, the foundation for social investment · A foundation that helps charities and social enterprises in England reach finance that mainstream investors do not offer.
  • Tribe Impact Capital: How we use the SDGs · Tribe's account of how the UN goals feed into ImpactDNA, the process a participant describes for drawing out a client's values.
  • Access: Blended finance · Access explains how it combines grant with repayable finance so that social investment funds can back organisations other investors see as too risky.

Reports and data

  • The UK impact investing market: Size, scope, and potential · The Impact Investing Institute's 2024 study puts the UK impact investing market at £76.8 billion at the end of 2023, the figure a participant cites.
  • Family Offices: A roadmap to impact · The Impact Investing Institute's guide for families and their advisers who want to start or deepen impact investing.
  • Evolving your endowment: Driving change through impact investing · The Impact Investing Institute's practical guide for charitable foundations that want their endowment to serve the same ends as their grants.

Law and policy

  • UN Sustainable Development Goals · The 17 goals that UN member states agreed in 2015, which Tribe uses to help clients state what matters to them.
  • Investing charity money: guidance for trustees (CC14) · The Charity Commission's guidance on financial and social investment sets the rules for any foundation in England and Wales that wants its portfolio to match its mission.

Books and ideas

  • The Water of Systems Change · The 2018 FSG paper by John Kania, Mark Kramer and Peter Senge on the conditions that hold a problem in place is recommended in the discussion as reading for catalytic investors.
  • The Fifth Discipline · Peter Senge's book on systems thinking and learning organisations is the best-known work of the author named in the discussion.
  • Catalytic Capital Consortium · The MacArthur Foundation's initiative defines catalytic capital as investment that accepts disproportionate risk or concessionary returns so that impact can happen.
  • Bridges Spectrum of Capital · Bridges Fund Management's widely used map of approaches from conventional investing to philanthropy gives a picture of the whole spectrum the session discusses.
  • Investor Contribution Strategies · Impact Frontiers sets out the shared norms on what an investor adds to an investment, the question behind a member's additionality test.
  • Blended finance · Convergence's primer covers the use of public or philanthropic money to draw private investment into a deal, the de-risking role a participant gives catalytic capital.

Further reading

  • Across the Returns Continuum · Omidyar Network's 2017 paper on when an investor should accept below-market returns speaks to the session's closing question about concessionary and market-rate capital.
  • Systemic Investing Practice Guide · The TransCap Initiative's guide offers methods for investors who want to fund change across a whole system and not only single deals.

To learn more or engage further on this topic, please reach out to Sam Underwood or Melanie Ormos.

Climate, Nature & Youth Leadership

  • Overview
  • Transcript
  • Links20

How can philanthropists fund young climate and nature leaders at the scale the problem needs?

A Forward Global facilitator sets out the gap: nearly half of members name climate or nature as an interest, while climate receives about 2% of philanthropy and less than 1% of climate funding reaches youth-led organisations. A participant describes a coalition of about 30 youth-led organisations with one theory of change and a shared ask of 10 million pounds. Another participant and a member explain how their foundation got past its doubts about funding young people. A second member describes Synchronicity Earth's trust-based funding of overlooked biodiversity work and its pooled funds. The open floor turns to climate messaging, social media, natural infrastructure, litigation and the cost of living.

Insights 12

Nearly half of Forward Global's members name climate or nature as an interest, while climate receives about 2% of philanthropy worldwideClimate and nature

The facilitator says about half of Forward Global's roughly 300 members name climate, nature, environment or conservation as an interest, yet climate still receives only about 2% of philanthropy. The initiative aims for a world where human norms, behaviours and systems are aligned with a stable climate and the flourishing of the natural world, and it offers a broad tent so members can step in without a fully formed strategy.01:41

About five funders give most of the environmental grant money from UK funders, in grants too small for whole-system workA participant · Climate and nature · The funder's role

A participant recommends the Environmental Funders Network's Where the Green Grants Went report. In her account of its findings, about five organisations and foundations give most UK climate and nature funding, which builds risk into the field. Funding is fragmented, typical grants of 10,000 to 20,000 pounds make whole-system change hard, and transport, waste, the circular economy and oceans are underfunded.08:18

Youth-led describes who runs an organisation, not the work the organisation doesA participant · Young leaders · The funder's role

A major UK funder turned Another Way down because the funder already backed a youth organisation. A participant asks whether the same funder would refuse a second grantee because it already funds one run by a 50-year-old white man. Youth-led groups range from climate musicals and festival DJ sets to local projects with young people. What the groups share is lived experience and a new way of seeing the world.10:12

A coalition of about 30 youth-led organisations plans to raise 10 million pounds together over three to five yearsA participant · Young leaders · Networks and collaboration

Young leaders mapped their shared system as a forest and wrote one theory of change around outcomes rather than single organisations. A participant says the coalition is designed for co-founding from the start, built on trust between leaders, and that several co-founders run their groups in the evening after a day job. The first ask is 10 million pounds, shared among the members. Another participant adds that about 30 organisations already work together for free.12:30

Funders who look for reasons not to back young leaders find those reasonsA participant · The funder's role · Young leaders

A participant says a family foundation listed every reason not to fund young leaders: too small, too risky, too fragmented, too inexperienced. In early meetings with another participant the foundation found evidence for its fears, "because that's what we chose to see". Watching the work grow changed the foundation's mind. Young people will live with the consequences longest, and they join up climate, nature, jobs and democracy.15:12

Small grants to small projects do not match a large problem, so funders and practitioners should plan togetherA member · The funder's role · Networks and collaboration

A member points to the 30 young leaders who designed their collective in 24 hours of joint work. She argues that giving small amounts to small projects makes no sense for a big issue. A group of funders and a group of practitioners can write the theory of change and the strategy together, and build a model for the work in a short time.20:02

Synchronicity Earth funds the gaps other funders avoid, and its founders' philanthropy covers the charity's own core costsA member · Climate and nature · The funder's role

A member says Synchronicity Earth began with biodiversity and then turned to the gaps: places and species that miss most funders' tick-box KPIs, from the Congo Basin and freshwater biodiversity to marine and Southeast Asian species. Seventeen years on it supports 160 partners on a baseline of trust. The founders' own philanthropy covers the core costs of Synchronicity Earth itself, which lowers the risk for other funders who come in.24:04

Pooled funds let funders back partners they would not fund directly, and a youth circle helps decide where biodiversity money goesA member · Networks and collaboration · Young leaders

A member describes one Synchronicity Earth pooled fund with 22 partners and 10 funders giving through it. Those funders would not give to the partners directly, but some do once they understand the work. Through the Chrysalis Youth Fund, a funding circle of young people advises on where biodiversity grants go.24:52

Nature belongs in every portfolio as a baseline, like an insurance policyA member · Climate and nature

A member notes that the Global Risks Report ranks biodiversity loss second over ten years, and argues that philanthropy should be the first mover. In her words, "nature touches everything", so whatever a funder's primary interest, supporting the natural world belongs in every portfolio as at least a baseline.32:36

Climate delay narratives are built on half-truths, so the answer to them has to be complex tooA participant · Climate and nature · Democracy and information

One member asks whether members should pool money for a simple five-year advertising campaign. A participant answers that fossil fuel lobbying has moved from denial to sowing doubt, with messages rooted in truth: individuals cannot make a difference, it is someone else's responsibility, it is unfair on working-class people. Another Way finds the same narratives in school textbooks, on TikTok and in classrooms, and helps young people take them apart through dialogue.33:47

People change because of those closest to them, more than because of a social media postA participant · Young leaders · Democracy and information

A participant says hate for climate activists on social media pushes young people out of school climate groups, and Another Way's own posts have been taken down. She cites social movement research showing that people are moved by those closest to them: "my family have gone vegan because of me." Community leaders and peers matter more than campaigns.47:07

Rivers that rise in upland peat have no value in financial markets, which one member wants to changeClimate and nature · Place and ownership

One member describes a rural place-based project where partners ask what it would take to classify a river system as natural infrastructure, the way roads or data centres are classed. The member says several rivers start in the area's peatland, yet financial markets do not recognise the river system as valuable and it has no protection. The partners also want a programme that finds young local talent and trains it in systems thinking to lead the new models.39:34

00:24On why climate funding lags member interest

Facilitator:We've been hearing from a number of members that this area is just too big. What can [one person] do? We see a lot of headlines; there are some positive ones too. So today we're going to have a really practical conversation.00:24

Facilitator:As part of the work that we've been doing in this initiative, we've worked with a number of members to set [our] directions. So maybe you heard one of these directions from the groups you're in, but for climate and nature, what we want to see across the world is that human norms, behaviours and systems are aligned with a stable climate and the flourishing of the natural world. That's what we believe can be. And yes, it is a little overwhelming, but we also know that capital can make [a huge difference]. That's why you're here today.01:05

Facilitator:To name it too, climate still only receives about 2% of [philanthropy]. And it's also one of the biggest interests within our own community. We did a survey of our own community, and of the 300 or so members that we have, nearly half named climate, nature, environment or conservation as an area of interest. Which is great. But that doesn't necessarily mean that everyone's doing something [in it], so I think that's a huge opportunity that we have.01:41

Facilitator:How do [we make it] easier to step into this space? Not everyone needs to have the most robust strategy. So that's what we're basically doing with this mission: providing a broad tent, thinking beyond climate mitigation, and really thinking about entire systems.02:39

Facilitator:As we did that community map, I wanted to name a few areas of interest that we saw across our own community. The first, Indigenous-led stewardship, being a really critical piece. Energy and [its] intersection with AI, food systems and regenerative agriculture, oceans and carbon, and conservation and biodiversity. That doesn't mean that's everything, but that's what we saw was a cluster of energy.03:03

Facilitator:And there are two areas that we pulled out that we found to be across all of these. One, [a] focus on narrative change: how is it that we talk about and understand the climate and what's happening, and also the role that we have to play within the solutions. And then two, investing in climate leaders and the future. So we're going to focus on that second piece today.03:31

Facilitator:I promise this isn't the last statistic I'm going to give you. Less than 1% of climate [funding] actually reaches [youth-led organisations]. There's just such an opportunity to invest in young people. And so what we want to talk about today is how might this community of ours do more here. That's the context.04:09

Facilitator:What I'd like to do next is I'm going to ask a few of you to share a few words. Then we're going to have space in the conversation, and we're going to have questions too.04:50

05:34On a youth-led coalition and its shared ask

Participant A:So I guess I'm going to tell you a little bit about what I do at Another Way, and how I see this moment and the opportunities. My work in the last 10 years has been around how we approach climate and environment education in a very holistic and systemic way: how we [create] internal and external conditions for young people to step in, and how we can dismantle the barriers that people face when it comes to taking action. So we've been working in a very intersectional way between education, skills, mental health, youth, and climate and nature.05:34

Participant A:So for me this poses a really interesting question of how we work together to create this kind of shared direction that we're all heading towards, and how we start to map our system. Member B:What was different was that, when he had set up his business, we were now receiving income from a structure he set up in order to generate funding for our foundation. Member B:So we focused on biodiversity, and then that was even massive in itself, and then it became the gaps, and what happens if we don't fund into those gaps. What are we left with? And the answer is a much less vibrant, less flourishing monoculture and society across the world.22:00

Member B:Our experience of funding globally for many, many years enabled us to learn and understand that we were never going to compete with local partners and knowledge, and we were always going to learn from their insights. Member B:I had a conversation with [one of the speakers]: are we catalytic? [Is ours] catalytic capital? Because I don't even know what the language is. Member B:So it's trying to draw attention to the things that somehow feel too impossible, too out of sight, that [seem] not going to result in anything meaningful. Member B:So 17 years on, we're supporting 160 partners across the world. Organisations and projects

  • Another Way · Another Way is a youth-led environmental education charity, working with teenagers in schools and communities across the UK.
  • Another Way: How we're re-energising the youth climate movement · Another Way's own account of the meeting where about 30 young climate leaders agree to work as one collective, the coalition a participant describes.
  • Power of 10 · Power of 10 is Another Way's app and community for teenagers who want to act for the planet, which a participant says is under threat from the social media ban.
  • Environmental Funders Network · The Environmental Funders Network is the UK network of foundations and donors who fund environmental work.
  • T. & J. Meyer Family Foundation · The Charity Commission's register entry for the foundation, a long-standing supporter of Another Way.
  • Synchronicity Earth · Synchronicity Earth is a UK charity, founded in 2009, that funds overlooked and underfunded biodiversity conservation around the world.
  • Synchronicity Earth: Pooled funds · Synchronicity Earth's pooled funds let donors combine their giving for locally led conservation groups, the model a member describes for bringing other funders in.
  • Chrysalis Youth Fund · The Chrysalis Youth Fund is Synchronicity Earth's pooled fund for young leaders and youth groups, with a committee of young people who recommend where grants go.
  • Forward Global: Initiatives · Forward Global describes its member-led Initiatives here, including Climate & Nature, whose direction and focus on young leaders the facilitator sets out at the start of the session.

Reports and data

  • Where the Green Grants Went 10 · The Environmental Funders Network's tenth analysis of UK environmental grants, published in November 2026, is the report a participant recommends and summarises.
  • The Global Risks Report 2026 · The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks ranks biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse second over ten years, behind extreme weather, which is the ranking a member cites.
  • Funding Trends 2026: Climate Change Mitigation Philanthropy · ClimateWorks Foundation's annual analysis finds that giving to climate change mitigation reached about 2.1% of global philanthropy in 2024, in line with the figure of about 2% quoted in the session.
  • Youth Climate Funding Study · The Youth Climate Justice Fund's two studies find that youth-led groups receive under 1% of grants from the largest climate foundations, the gap the facilitator names.
  • Global trends in climate change litigation: 2026 snapshot · The Grantham Research Institute's yearly review of climate lawsuits worldwide covers cases that seek damages from fossil fuel companies, a route raised in the open floor.

Law and policy

  • Growing up in the online world: a national consultation · The UK government's consultation outcome sets out its plan to ban social media companies from offering their services to under-16s, the ban a participant says puts Another Way's app for teenagers at risk.

Books and ideas

  • Discourses of climate delay · This open-access paper by William Lamb and colleagues maps the arguments that accept climate change but justify inaction, the move from denial to doubt and delay that a participant describes.
  • Explainer: What are debt-for-nature swaps? · Dialogue Earth explains the deals that reduce a country's debt in return for conservation commitments, one of the routes beyond grants raised in the open floor.

Further reading

  • Ecologies of Empowerment: Funding youth-led biodiversity action · Synchronicity Earth's summary of a report made with the Global Youth Biodiversity Network finds that most young conservation leaders work as volunteers without adequate funding.
  • Britain Talks Climate · Climate Outreach's research on how different groups of the British public think and talk about climate change gives background to the debate about simple and complex messages.
  • The Economics of Biodiversity: The Dasgupta Review · The independent review for the UK Treasury argues that economies treat nature as free and should count it as an asset, the idea behind the open floor discussion of rivers as natural infrastructure.

To learn more or engage further on this topic, please reach out to Sam Underwood or Melanie Ormos.

AI Safety & Power Concentration

  • Overview
  • Transcript
  • Links22

What can philanthropy do while AI moves faster than almost anyone expected?

A Forward Global facilitator interviews a participant who works on making AI safer. He cites a METR assessment that found one leading lab improving its models about twice as fast as before, and argues that concentration of power, in companies, in governments and between countries, is the likelier and less funded risk. A member calls for far more independent auditing of frontier labs and presents a member-backed fund that prepares policy, verification and institutions for a possible warning shot. Floor speakers raise data centres, governance failure, game theory and open-source models. The close turns to how donors can choose trusted partners and move money quickly.

Insights 12

AI capability at one leading lab is improving about twice as fast as before, METR findsA participant · AI and technology

A participant cites a recent METR report as finding that AI capability improved twice as fast over the past year as expected, mainly because existing models now write about 80% of the code for new ones. [METR's November 2026 assessment covers one lab, Anthropic. It estimates that the lab's models are improving at about twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025, and guesses that about 80% of that acceleration comes from the lab's use of AI in research and development. It gives no figure for the share of code written by AI.] He says this moves the field toward recursive self-improvement, where AI builds better AI around the clock, and that limits on compute and data centres are now less likely to slow development.00:00

Concentration of power is a likelier AI risk than loss of control, and philanthropy funds it far lessA participant · AI and technology · Democracy and information

Most philanthropic money for AI risk goes to making the AI itself safe. a participant argues that concentration of power is both more neglected and more likely: few people want an AI that disempowers everyone, but many want an AI that helps them consolidate their own power. That problem remains even if alignment is solved, and the field is still working out how to define it.04:02

AI power could concentrate in a few companies, in governments or in two dominant countriesA participant · AI and technology · Democracy and information

A participant sees three routes. AI companies could end up producing most economic output by automating labour, which would change the political settlement as well as the economy. Governments, starting with the US, treat the labs as strategic and use AI to widen surveillance. And the US and China could become so dominant that Europe and other middle powers lose any say over how the world is run.05:08

The UK and Europe can act on AI power through sovereign compute, observatories and civil-liberties groupsA participant · AI and technology · Democracy and information

A participant names three options for middle powers. Sovereign access to compute means no other country can switch off access to AI. Observatories can track where power is concentrating and raise the salience of the problem early. And civil-liberties organisations can take up AI in their own work. He calls the monitoring and awareness work cheap to do and a powerful use of philanthropic money.08:23

Donors anywhere can help start a tenfold increase in independent audits of frontier AI labsA member · AI and technology

A member argues that where donors live does not limit where they can act, and much of the power over AI sits in the US. He says the labs are not transparent and that their most capable models are deployed internally, out of public view. He calls for at least ten times more third-party auditing inside the labs, which philanthropy can start, so that the public and politicians understand what these models can do.11:13

Data centres make the harms of AI concrete for people todayAI and technology · Climate and nature

One member says data centres turn tech power into something everyone can see: emissions that put carbon targets out of reach, higher costs and pollution for nearby communities, the heaviest burden on marginalised communities, and questions about surveillance. Opposition to the build-out unites many movements at once. The same member points to competition policy and the EU Digital Markets Act as tools against present-day concentration of power.19:12

Fewer data centres in the US slows dangerous AI, but middle powers still need compute of their ownA member · AI and technology

A member holds both views at once. More data centres in the US means more capacity to train more dangerous models, so he wants fewer there. But he does not want the UK, Canada and other middle powers left without compute in an economy that runs on AI. Since the compute will be built somewhere, he would rather it go to democracies with clean energy than to authoritarian states.21:52

Verification of what runs on data-centre chips can make AI agreements between rival nations holdA participant · AI and technology · Democracy and information

Asked whether competition between nations makes AI regulation impossible, a participant says the race is closer to a stag hunt than a prisoner's dilemma: if each side can verify what the others run on their data-centre chips, every side has a reason to cooperate. The technical barriers to that verification are real but solvable, and solving them makes international or bilateral agreements much easier to reach.34:03

A member-backed AI fund builds what policymakers would need after a warning shotA member · AI and technology · Democracy and information

The fund a member helped set up works backwards from a possible warning shot, a disaster that wakes the world up. It backs auditing, AI expertise in US congressional offices, verification technology and a founder designing the body to run an international AI agreement. A participant says people in the EU AI Office told him the institution was not planned before the EU AI Act, and he passes on the founder's insight: "You don't just have the law, you have to have the institution that enforces it." A second strand covers power shifting from labour to compute.40:44

Donors in AI safety have to choose trusted partners quickly and give at full size the first timeA member · The funder's role · AI and technology

Philanthropy usually spends time mapping a field and making small learning grants. A member says AI does not allow that time: donors have to decide quickly whom to trust and write the right cheque to the right organisation the first time. Partner organisations report funding gaps of tens to hundreds of millions of dollars, and his fund spends each round of funding within three months instead of holding an endowment.46:20

A youth organisation in Brixton is setting up a community AI lab for young people excluded from mainstream educationAI and technology · Young leaders

One member supports a south London organisation that works with young people excluded from mainstream education and is setting up what the member describes as the UK's first community-powered youth AI lab. The organisation meets young people where they already are: a place they go after school, one of the few neutral places where rival gangs can meet without risk of knife crime.43:33

The line between today's AI harms and future AI risks is breaking downA participant · AI and technology · Rupture and emergence

A participant says the split between present harms and future risks no longer holds: surveillance infrastructure is being installed now, and AI may reach superhuman capability by the end of next year. Funders who focus on the highest-impact options, or find a trusted adviser, can make a large difference. "The future is not set in stone. There are many different paths that this could take. Some of them are really, really good paths."51:18

00:00On how fast AI capability is growing

Participant A:What they [METR] found was that the capability had been improving twice as fast as they had previously expected over the last year. And the primary driver of this was that about 80% of the code on new models has been written by existing AI models. And so this is tipping us toward a kind of inflection point, which is called recursive self-improvement, which is basically where AI models are doing all the work to build better AI models. And many people expect that when you hit this point, what we would have is essentially a very, very fast takeoff, where you have models working around the clock, obviously they don't need to stop, and they're building a better model which is then building a better model again. [METR's November 2026 assessment covers one lab, Anthropic. It estimates progress at about twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025 and attributes about 80% of that acceleration to the lab's use of AI in research and development. It gives no figure for the share of code written by AI.]00:00

Participant A:And so if this is possible, and there are still some people who think that there are technical reasons why you might not achieve this, then we really don't know how fast or how far this technology will go. But already, even just being able to move twice as quickly, even without RSI, it means that we're then at a place where maybe every three months you're doubling the capability of the model. And critically, this has been done also by finding new ways to design the [inaudible], which means even some of the things like the amount of computing, how many data centres are being built, which could have been a bottleneck, are much less likely to slow down the development of AI.00:42

Participant A:So we are losing some of the levers we might have had to slow down AI outside of regulation, and it's much faster than almost everybody anticipated. A lot of people are still thinking about what this ultimately means, but we are in a world that is much, much faster than we thought in October.01:25

Member A:Maybe one [thing] I can add here. And by that they meant has a reasonable chance of causing human extinction. And over 10% of researchers at that time thought this was possible. [The AI Impacts surveys of AI researchers report this the other way round: about half of those surveyed put the chance of an outcome as bad as human extinction at 10% or more.]01:49

Member A:And it just occurred to me: if I was going to get on an airplane, and right before it took off I [learned] 10% of the engineers who built that airplane thought it was going to crash, I'm not going to get on that airplane. Participant A:Yeah, so power concentration is, I think, a really fascinating area, because the vast majority of philanthropic money that is going into trying to reduce AI risk is going into mainly trying to make the AI itself safe, so the loss of control problem. So this is one of the areas that is more neglected, and I think actually a more likely risk. Because there is[n't] an interest to build an AI that takes over and disempowers everybody. There's quite a lot of people's interest to have an AI that allows them to consolidate their power, to increase power. Participant A:So a priori, I think this is a much more likely risk. Participant A:So one is AI companies themselves consolidate power: the vast majority of all economic production is a result of these few AI companies. There's a huge amount of economic power. Participant A:And then the third way that you can have concentration is between countries. Participant A:And we see the trilateral meetings between China, the US and Russia at the moment. Organisations and projects

  • Catalyze Impact · Incubator that helps experienced founders start organisations working to make AI safe.
  • Ark Philanthropy · An advisory and grantmaking organisation that incubates multi-donor funds and treats rapid AI progress as a working assumption.
  • METR · Independent research organisation that evaluates frontier AI models and publishes the report on AI progress that a participant cites.
  • European AI Office · The European Commission body that enforces the AI Act's rules for general-purpose models, used in the session as the example of an institution that was not ready when its law passed.
  • Anthropic: statement on the Department of War discussions · Anthropic's February 2026 statement that it will not allow its models to be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance, the refusal a participant points to when he compares closed and open-source models.

Reports and data

  • METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026 · The November 2026 assessment that estimates model progress at about twice its earlier rate and attributes most of the speed-up to AI itself, the report a participant opens with and a member tells donors to read.
  • METR: investigation of the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident · METR's independent account of the July 2026 incident in which about 700 AI agents from an OpenAI evaluation joined an attack on Hugging Face, which a member counts as an early warning shot.
  • Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI · A survey of 2,778 AI researchers in which between 38% and 51% give at least a 10% chance to outcomes as bad as human extinction, the kind of finding behind a member's aeroplane comparison.
  • International AI Safety Report 2026 · The international scientific review of the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI, led by Yoshua Bengio, which sets out the evidence behind the risks discussed here.
  • From a Welfare State to a Working State: the Milburn review of young people and work · Alan Milburn's 278-page report for the UK government on young people not in education, employment or training, published in November 2026 and cited in the session for giving AI a page and a half.
  • Carbon Brief: five charts on data-centre energy use and emissions · An explainer built on International Energy Agency data showing how much electricity data centres use now and are projected to use by 2030, the figures disputed from the floor.

Law and policy

  • EU AI Act · The European Union's risk-based law on AI, which the speakers cite to show that a law struggles when the body meant to enforce it is not built in advance.
  • EU Digital Markets Act · The EU law that sets obligations for the largest platforms, named from the floor as a tool for limiting the concentration of tech power that already exists.
  • Chemical Weapons Convention · The treaty banning chemical weapons, run by its own standing organisation, which a participant gives as the model for an institution that could monitor an international AI agreement.
  • UK Compute Roadmap · The UK government's plan for building public and private computing capacity for AI, the policy area behind a participant's call for sovereign access to compute.

Books and ideas

  • Yoshua Bengio's speech at the UN Security Council · The September 2026 address in which Yoshua Bengio names catastrophic misuse, concentration of power and loss of control as the three global threats from frontier AI, the framing the facilitator uses to open the discussion.
  • Recursive self-improvement · The idea that AI systems could do the work of building better AI systems, which a participant describes as the inflection point the field is approaching.
  • Stag hunt · The game theory model in which everyone gains from cooperating once each side trusts the others to do the same, which a participant prefers to the prisoner's dilemma as a picture of the AI race.

Further reading

  • AI-Enabled Coups: How a Small Group Could Use AI to Seize Power · Forethought's report on how advanced AI could help a small group take illegitimate power and what could prevent it, a fuller treatment of the risk a participant calls neglected.
  • AI Behind Closed Doors: a Primer on the Governance of Internal Deployment · Apollo Research's primer on the risks of AI models that labs use internally before any public release, the gap a member wants independent auditors to close.
  • Verification for International AI Governance · A report from the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative on how countries could check each other's compliance with AI agreements, the technical problem both speakers say has to be solved.
  • Gradual Disempowerment · A paper arguing that people could lose influence over the economy, culture and the state step by step as AI replaces human work, close to the fund's second strand on power moving from labour to compute.

To learn more or engage further on this topic, please reach out to Sam Underwood or Melanie Ormos.

European Gathering 2026 › Working group

The Information Environment

  • Overview
  • In their wordsQuotes6
  • Links12

What would it take to rebuild trust in democracy when the information people rely on is under pressure?

Members start from a diagnosis: trust has broken down between the state and citizens, among citizens, and in institutions, while the supply chain for information has been neglected. One account traces a philanthropy-backed campaign that shaped the UK's Online Safety Act and, by that member's account, measures in the EU and Australia and a bill before Canada's parliament, with the lesson that every win has to be defended when the rules are put into practice. Others warn that AI search and summaries can change what people are able to check as true. A second thread treats local news as democratic infrastructure and sets out the funding each stage of rebuilding it needs. Members also point to small local campaigns that hold power to account.

Insights 8

Democracy is under strain because trust has collapsed between the state and citizens, between citizens, and in institutions.Democracy and information

One member describes democracy as a set of relationships: between state and citizen, between citizens and institutions, and between citizens themselves. All three are failing at once. Trust in institutions has collapsed, and so, to a degree, has trust in people who do not come from the same place or look the same. Another member adds that democracy cannot function without healthy relationships in those spaces.

Information has a supply chain like food or medicine, and it has been neglected while political pressure on it grows.Democracy and information

Societies govern the supply chains for food, pharmaceuticals and weapons, but neglected the one for information for a long time, one member argues, and that supply chain is now under attack. In 2024, a senior US politician tied American support for NATO to how Europe treated a platform owner, and a presidential candidate threatened a tech chief executive with prison over the coming election. The member reads both as signs that the contest over information had raised its stakes.

Philanthropy-backed work on online safety in the UK fed into the Online Safety Act, and a member says it travelled abroad.Democracy and information

Philanthropic funding backed work setting out how platforms could be regulated to protect children and marginalised groups, and that work fed into the UK's Online Safety Act. By one member's account it also informed the EU's Digital Services Act, Australian regulation, a bill now before Canada's parliament and the US Kids Online Safety Act. The plan was a "bank shot strategy": make the law work in the UK first, then use it as proof elsewhere.

A policy victory has to be defended for years, because implementation is where companies win back ground.Democracy and information · The funder's role

The online safety campaign won its early battles, but the lesson drawn from it is that a new law is only the start. Companies fight over how the rules are applied, and the ground gained in parliament can be lost in implementation. The advice to funders and organisers: "You have to remember, when you have any victories, you have to win the win."

AI search and summaries threaten people's ability to check what was actually true.AI and technology · Democracy and information

Members warn that AI search summaries give people what the system thinks they want to know, with no incentive to tell the truth. One says access to frontier AI is subsidised by venture capital, so journalists and the public may lose it when prices rise. Another says AI changes material after the fact, leaving researchers and citizens unable to verify the original record. One response under way is a new top-level domain with access controls, meant as a global reserve of knowledge that AI has not altered.

Local news is democratic infrastructure, and the aim is one reliable source in each of the UK's 361 local authority districts.Democracy and information · Place and ownership

Local media did more civic work than anyone noticed while it was strong. As its business model collapsed over the first quarter of this century, democracy, belonging and shared reality all came under pressure. Local news brings people back into a shared reality and helps them hold power to account. A district typically has about 165,000 people, one member says, the size of a mid-sized town or city borough, and about 4.4 million people in the UK live in districts with no dedicated local news outlet.

Rebuilding local news needs three stages of funding, and the first and last stages are the hardest to fund.Democracy and information · Capital and investment

One member sets out a three-stage model. Incubate new outlets from scratch in news deserts. Accelerate the promising ones until they are investment ready. Then catalyse, bringing in impact capital from institutional investors, social investors and government. Incubation comes first but is the harder work, and catalytic capital is the gap that institutions and government are best placed to fill.

Funding small local campaign groups helps people rebuild trust and hold those in power to account.Democracy and information

Members point to small community groups that fight back where people sense impunity among tech and political elites: parents urging other parents to wait until children are 16 before giving them smartphones, and mothers challenging their local hospital over maternity deaths. Such groups are multiplying across Britain. Members also call for educating MPs and peers on corporate interests, including private equity in public services, and for political finance reform, after one party received £72 million from two donors.

Reports and data

  • Pew Research Center: do people click on links in Google AI summaries? · A 2025 analysis finding that people who see an AI summary in Google search click through to a source about half as often, evidence for the worry about AI summaries raised in the session.
  • News Integrity in AI Assistants · A 2025 European Broadcasting Union and BBC study finding that almost half of AI assistants' answers about the news have at least one significant problem, which bears on the warning that AI systems have no incentive to tell the truth.
  • National Maternity and Neonatal Investigation: final reports · The 2026 independent investigation into maternity and neonatal care in England, the national picture behind the local groups described as challenging hospitals over maternity deaths.

Law and policy

  • Online Safety Act 2023 · The UK law that places duties on online platforms to protect users, especially children, and the law the campaign described in the session led to.
  • EU Digital Services Act · The European Commission's guide to the EU law on platform accountability, which one member says the UK campaign fed into directly.
  • Australia: Digital Duty of Care · The Australian government's page on legislation introduced in October 2026 that would require online services to take reasonable steps to keep users safe, the Australian regulation one member says the campaign inspired.
  • Canada: Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act · The Canadian bill introduced in June 2026 that would give social media services a duty to act responsibly and create a Digital Safety Commission, the bill before Canada's parliament mentioned in the session.
  • US Kids Online Safety Act (S.1748) · The US Senate bill on protecting children online, now before Congress again, which one member says draws on the same campaign.
  • Amplify: The Local Media Action Plan · The UK government's 2026 plan for local news, which reports that up to 37 local authority districts have no dedicated outlet and as many as 4.4 million people live in local news deserts.
  • Representation of the People Bill: policy summaries · The UK government's summaries of its elections bill, including its political finance measures, the area of reform members call for.

Network principles and practice

  • Overview
  • In their wordsQuotes7
  • Links11

What changes when funders and organisations work through networks instead of growing their own organisations?

A member sets out the four principles her research finds in high-impact networks: mission before organisation, trust not control, humility not brand, and constellations not stars. Co-leads and members then test them against practice. A participant describes how Flying Labs gives local experts ownership in more than 35 countries and governs through clear boundaries instead of control. North Star Transition convenes more than 200 stakeholders in South Wales around river pollution. Members discuss how to show impact when outcomes come from many hands: measure contribution, keep one North Star metric, and avoid networks that exist only to convene. Stories of an online safety campaign and of early backing for young pioneers show the same principles at work.

Insights 7

High-impact networks share four principles: mission before organisation, trust not control, humility not brand, and constellations not stars.A member · Networks and collaboration

A member finds the same leadership mindset across the high-impact networks she has studied for more than twenty years. People put the mission ahead of their organisation's self-interest and give up control when needed. They govern through trust, finding partners with shared values and then letting go. They share credit generously, which builds a reserve of goodwill for future collaboration. And they build constellations instead of little empires, because social change is complex, emergent and messy.

Network leaders nudge direction from behind and judge impact by their contribution instead of claiming credit.Networks and collaboration

One member compares network leadership to "a cowboy at the back of the herd": the herd knows roughly where it is going, and the leader nudges it back on course now and then. Members say impact in networks should be shown as contribution rather than attribution, since relationships are hard to measure and system change often fails. They advise keeping at least one simple North Star metric, avoiding networks that exist only to convene, and collecting data in ways that strengthen the network.

Flying Labs puts local experts in charge in more than 35 countries, and the network's interdependence makes it resilient.A participant · Networks and collaboration · AI and technology

A participant describes a network of local experts who own, decide on and lead the use of drones, data and geospatial AI in their own countries, and help to finance it. The central organisation stays small because its job is to bring people together, not to control them. Partners are neither dependent nor independent but interdependent, so when a funding shock hits one country, no single node is critical and other partners step in.

Clear, transparent boundaries let network partners hold each other to account without control from the top.A participant · Networks and collaboration

Flying Labs keeps strengthening its network boundaries: transparent guidelines on what it means to be part of the network. Partners pay a small annual fee for access to shared resources and commit to the network's two values, sharing and collaboration. Each year partners assess themselves against those expectations. A participant finds that peers then hold each other accountable, which works better than oversight from the centre and lets the centre give up decision-making.

A campaign that hands the credit to its partners builds a broader coalition.Networks and collaboration · Democracy and information

One member describes an online safety campaign that built a wide coalition by giving smaller campaigns free help, including legal advice, and by sending journalists to speak to its grantees instead of to the funder. The member says the method has since been used by campaigns on social media regulation in other countries.

In South Wales, North Star Transition reframed river pollution as a question of how local businesses work.Networks and collaboration · Climate and nature

North Star Transition set up a Transition Lab that, by the account given in the room, brought together more than 200 stakeholders from farming, the environment, the NHS, energy and transport to decide what they want to change in their region. The lab's framing: "It's not about the rivers. It's about the business practice of people who live around the rivers." The network brought two development banks together, which set up a broad loan for farm transitions, and North Star has never claimed the credit.

Backing young people's ideas early can build a network of future leaders that a funder only sees years later.Young leaders · The funder's role

One member describes a fund where young people can bring an idea. Years later, every group the member's network went on to fund was run by someone who had started in that fund. Funding people and leadership early, as well as projects, builds a network before anyone knows it exists.

Networks and collaboration

Organisations and projects

  • The New Network Leader · A resource site that sets out the four principles of network leadership, with case studies, articles and webinars.
  • WeRobotics · The nonprofit that acts as steward of the Flying Labs network instead of directing it from the centre.
  • Flying Labs · This network of locally led drone, data and AI labs across Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and Asia-Pacific is a participant's example of interdependence.
  • North Star Transition · An organisation that convenes people from across a whole system in Transition Labs to agree what they want to change and how to pay for it.
  • Wye-Usk Transition Lab · North Star Transition describes the first phase of its lab in the Wye and Usk river catchments, which treats farming, river pollution, health, energy and transport as one system.
  • 10,000 Days (Hope Initiatives International) · The 10,000 Days plan commits its author to another 10,000 days of projects on climate justice, racial justice, and peace and reconciliation.

Reports and data

  • Four Network Principles for Collaboration Success · A 2013 article in The Foundation Review that draws the four principles from a decade of case studies of successful networks.

Law and policy

  • Online Safety Act 2023 · This is the UK law setting safety duties for online platforms, which the coalition campaign described in the session helped to shape.

Books and ideas

  • The Networked Nonprofit · A 2008 article in Stanford Social Innovation Review that argues nonprofits achieve more by investing in trusted networks than by growing themselves.
  • Contribution analysis · This evaluation approach, first set out by John Mayne, shows what an intervention contributed to a result without claiming sole credit, which is the shift members ask for in measuring networks.

Further reading

  • Cracking the Network Code: Four Principles for Grantmakers · This 2013 guide from Grantmakers for Effective Organizations applies the four network principles to the choices funders make.
